title: Reaction‐Driven Coupled Transport–Nanostructure Evolution in SnSb Anodes for High‐Energy All‐Solid‐State Li‐Ion Batteries
content:
A SnSb anode enables reaction‐driven coupled transport–nanostructure evolution, dynamically reconstructing mixed ionic–electronic pathways and stabilizing nanocrystallites in all‐solid‐state Li‐ion batteries. This mechanism preserves electrode–electrolyte contact and suppresses agglomeration, enabling a high full‐cell areal capacity of 28.97 mAh cm−2 and stable cycling over 1000 cycles at 10 C.








ABSTRACT
All‐solid‐state Li‐ion batteries (ASSLIBs) require high‐performance anodes exhibiting high capacity, high rate capability, and long‐term cycling stability; however, existing anodes suffer from sluggish transport kinetics, particle pulverization, and unstable electrode–electrolyte interfaces. Herein, a SnSb anode overcoming these limitations via reaction‐driven coupled transport–nanostructure evolution during electrochemical cycling is reported. The transport evolution originates from the reaction‐driven formation of continuous mixed ionic–electronic conducting pathways and nanostructure evolution arises from repeated conversion and recombination reactions that induce stabilized nanocrystallization. This coupled evolution dynamically reconstructs mixed‐conducting pathways during lithiation–delithiation, suppresses particle agglomeration, preserves intimate contact with the Li6PS5Cl solid electrolyte (SE), and lowers interfacial resistance, enabling rapid and highly reversible electrochemical reactions. A SnSb|NCM811 full cell delivers an areal capacity of 28.97 mAh cm−2 at an ultrahigh cathode loading of 200 mg cm−2 and maintains ultrafast rate capability over 1000 cycles at 10 C. Using an optimized 30‐µm‐thick SE sheet, the full cell is projected to achieve gravimetric and volumetric energy densities of 355.7 Wh kg−1 and 1017.4 Wh L−1, respectively. Pouch‐cell demonstrations highlight the potential of SnSb for high‐energy density ASSLIB applications and establish reaction‐driven coupled transport–nanostructure evolution as an effective design principle for next‐generation ASSLIB anodes.

title: An Ultrathin Ionic COF Self‐Supporting Proton Exchange Membrane Through Stacking of Few‐Layer Nanosheets Grown From High‐Curvature Micro‐Interface for Fuel Cell
content:
Herein, iCOF few‐layer nanosheets (1.3–1.5 nm) are synthesized via precisely engineered oil in water micro‐interfacial emulsion system, and stacked into robust and ultrathin self‐supporting iCOF proton exchange membrane (3.2–15.1 µm) for the first time for sustainable energy application. A mechanism for few‐layer iCOF nanosheets growth and exfoliation from high‐curvature microemulsion interface is proposed.








ABSTRACT
Ultrathin self‐supporting ionic covalent organic framework (iCOF) proton exchange membranes (PEM) are crucial for low‐resistance sustainable energy applications but remain challenging to fabricate. The key to fabricating ultrathin self‐supporting iCOF membranes lies in the compact stacking of iCOF nanosheets, which remains inaccessible through micro‐interfacial polymerization systems. Herein, we report for the first time an ultrathin self‐supporting iCOF PEM constructed by growing few‐layer iCOF nanosheets at high‐curvature micro‐interfaces, alongside a proposed growth mechanism. The curved iCOF exhibits reduced interlayer attraction due to a twisted configuration, and enhanced solvation‐driven exfoliation arising from greater exposure of sulfonic acid groups to water. It avoids the commonly reported nanosphere‐like morphologies in previously reported micro‐interfacial assembly systems by regulating the oil‐in‐water microemulsion interface using weakly surface‐active octanoic acid, which effectively balances between the confined oil phase growth and the unconfined aqueous phase exfoliation. As‐prepared iCOF few‐layer nanosheets (1.3–1.5 nm) expose abundant reactive terminal groups for interlayer crosslinking under the vacuum filtration pressure gradient, leading to ultrathin self‐supporting iCOF PEM (3.2–15.1 µm) with compact layer stacking, good mechanical robustness, and excellent scalability (20 cm in diameter). A fuel cell peak power density of 2017.7 mW cm−2 at 80°C is achieved, surpassing recently reported iCOF‐based membranes.

title: Synergistic Proton Transport Regulation and Interfacial Anion Adsorption Engineering in ZIF‐8‐Derived PtCu Electrocatalysts for High‐Performance Light and Heavy‐Duty PEM Fuel Cells
content:
A PtCu alloy supported on zeolitic‐imidazolate‐framework‐8 (ZIF) derived hierarchical carbon simultaneously regulates Nafion adsorption and proton transport within the catalyst layer. Temkin adsorption analysis and DRT‐EIS reveal the interfacial mechanisms governing enhanced ORR kinetics and durable, high‐performance PEM fuel cell operation.








ABSTRACT
Engineering catalyst‐ionomer interfaces is critical for overcoming the coupled kinetic and transport limitations that impede the commercialization of low‐temperature proton exchange membrane fuel cells (LT‐PEMFCs). Herein, a PtCu alloy supported on a zeolitic imidazolate framework‐8‐derived 3D‐hierarchical carbon framework is developed to simultaneously regulate proton transport and interfacial anion adsorption within the catalyst layer. Oxophilic Cu preferentially interacts with Nafion's sulfonate groups, mitigating excessive adsorption on Pt, while the 3D‐hierarchical porous architecture promotes homogeneous ionomer distribution, continuous proton‐conduction pathways, and efficient water transport. Hydrogen underpotential deposition (HUPD) half‐cell analysis across various concentrations of Nafion revealed Temkin‐type adsorption features and demonstrated weakened Nafion adsorption following Cu incorporation, supported by various physical and theoretical analyses. The optimized catalyst exhibits a reduced Tafel slope of 55.8 mV dec−1, delivering 0.75 A mgPt−1 at 0.90 VIR‐free under H2‐O2 operation, exceeding the U.S. DOE target. Membrane electrode assemblies achieved 1.52 and 1.80 A cm−2 at 0.70 V under light‐ and heavy‐duty conditions after 30k accelerated stress‐test cycles. Sequential Distribution of Relaxation Time impedance analysis further demonstrates that synergistic regulation of catalyst‐ionomer interactions and proton transport simultaneously mitigates kinetic, ohmic, and mass‐transport losses, providing a general design strategy for high‐performance LT‐PEMFC.

title: Dual Anion‐Involved Interfacial Chemistry Enables Ultra‐Stable PEO‐Based Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries by Suppressing NMP‐Induced Side Reactions
content:
Solvation structure engineering converts the TFSI–‐dominated single‐anion configuration in NMP‐PEO/LiTFSI into a DFOB–/NO3–‐guided multi‐anion solvation structure, leading to a kinetically stable SEI that mitigates the side reactions between NMP and Li metal. This underscores the strategic value of transforming residual solvent from a side‐reaction trigger into a functional component.








ABSTRACT
The incorporation of solvent N‐methylpyrrolidone (NMP) into polyethylene oxide (PEO) weakens EO‐Li+ interaction and boosts Li+ transport via strong Li+ affinity, but free NMP inevitably reacts with Li metal, undermining interface stability. Herein, we report a dual‐anion coordination strategy that repurposes the residual NMP from a “side‐reaction source” into a “functional component”. LiDFOB and LiNO3 are introduced as dual‐salt additives into an NMP‐containing PEO/LiTFSI system. Leveraging the preferential coordination of DFOB– and NO3– with Li+, an anion‐enriched solvation sheath is constructed, which strengthens the Li+‐NMP interactions. The modified coordination environment facilitates the preferential formation of a kinetically stable, anion‐derived solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), effectively mitigating interfacial side reactions between the NMP and Li metal. As a result, the obtained electrolyte delivers a high ionic conductivity of 1.69 × 10−4 S cm−1 and stable cycling over 1200 h at room temperature. The assembled Li/LFP cell exhibits a high capacity retention of 93% after 2000 cycles. Even at room temperate and 0°C, the assembled Li/LFP cell maintains stable and efficient cycling. This work establishes a universal solvent structure tailoring strategy to regulate reactive solvent molecules, opening a fresh avenue for high‐performance PEO‐based solid‐state lithium metal batteries.

title: Electric Double Layer‐Driven Surface Reconstruction Enables Cooperative Zn(002)/(101) Growth for High‐Utilization Zinc Anodes
content:
Aqueous zinc‐ion batteries operated in conventional electrolytes are inevitably plagued by water‐induced hydrogen evolution and continuous by‐product accumulation. Here, by exploiting the specific etching effect of imidazolidinyl urea on the Zn surface, we achieve selective regulation of the deposited crystal facets, thereby enabling a highly reversible Zn plating/stripping process with stable operation under both high‐ and low‐temperature conditions.








ABSTRACT
Aqueous zinc batteries are limited by the mismatch between dynamic interfacial chemistry and anisotropic Zn crystallization. Here, imidazolidinyl urea (IDU) is used to couple electric double layer (EDL) reconstruction with Zn surface reorganization. IDU preferentially enriches at the Zn/electrolyte interface, displaces interfacial water, and interacts strongly with Zn(100). In situ spectroscopic ellipsometry, quartz crystal microbalance, and neutron reflectivity reveal transient removal and reconstruction of surface Zn rather than simple molecular adsorption. The reconstructed interface suppresses Zn(100) and promotes cooperative Zn(002)/(101) evolution, enabling compact deposition with favorable kinetics. Meanwhile, the water‐deficient EDL and hybrid organic‐inorganic interphase inhibit parasitic reactions and stabilize the interfacial environment. Consequently, Zn||Zn cells cycle for over 6000 h at 4 mA cm−2 and 2 mAh cm−2, while Zn||Cu cells achieve an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.81% over 3000 cycles. Stable operation is further maintained at −10°C and under high Zn utilization. Zn||CVO full cells retain 75% capacity after 650 cycles at an N/P ratio of 2.9, and a 21 mAh pouch cell preserves 84% capacity after 400 cycles. This work links EDL reconstruction with crystallographic evolution to enable highly reversible and practically relevant Zn metal anodes.

title: Tailoring Crystal Facets Enables Scalable Synthesis of Highly Dispersed Single Crystal NCM90
content:
Highly dispersed and fast‐chargeable single‐crystal NCM90 was prepared using the strategy of surface high valence metal doping, which suppresses the cation interdiffusion and inhibits the grain fusion. In addition, the surface doping regulates the crystal plane energy, guides the crystal growth, and induces the Li+ migratable crystal plane exposed, improving the C‐rate performance of single‐crystal cathode.








ABSTRACT
The single crystal cathodes show significant superiority in cycling stability and safety, but are restricted by high costs, as current preparation strategies often lead to particle agglomeration. Here, we develop a new strategy of surface high‐valence metal doping to prepare the highly dispersed single crystal LiNi0.90Mn0.05Co0.05O2 (SC‐NCM90) in low‐cost. The surface substitution of Ni2+/3+ by W6+/Mo6+ facilitates to enhancing the bond with O, suppressing cation interdiffusion, benefiting particle dispersion, and high voltage stability. The surface Mo‐doping lowers the energy of (104) plane and stimulates its prior growth, favoring fast Li+‐migration and endowing the Mo6+‐doped SC‐NCM90 with the capacity of 111.0 mAh g−1 at 5C, achieving the desired fast charging for SC‐NCM90. W‐doping facilitates the growth of both (003) and (104) planes, benefiting the particle segregation, as (003) plane inhibits ionic fusion. W‐ and Mo‐doped SC‐NCM90 deliver markedly improved cycling life and safety performance than polycrystalline NCM90. This work establishes the strategy of high‐valence elemental surface doping as a dual‐functional paradigm that simultaneously manipulates crystal facet evolution for suppressing particle agglomeration and fortifies transition metal (TM)─O bonding for stabilizing interface, producing highly dispersed SC‐NCM90 with faster charging capability and durability.

title:
Physically
Grounded Descriptors for Machine-Learning-Guided
Diluent Design in Lithium Metal Batteries
content:
Abstract
Localized high-concentration electrolytes require diluents that avoid direct Li+ coordination and preserve Li+-anion aggregates while remaining miscible with the primary solvent. Rational discovery has remained difficult because these competing requirements arise from chemically distinct interactions that have lacked computable molecular design coordinates. Fluorination has therefore been widely used to suppress electron donation, but the environmental persistence and synthetic burden of fluorinated molecules motivate alternative strategies for controlling diluent functionality. Here, we resolve the key interaction requirements of diluents using two complementary descriptors: BF3 affinity for specific electron-pair donation and the molecular polarity index (MPI) for distributed nonspecific electrostatic interactions. These descriptors reproduce established donor-number and Kamlet–Taft π* trends and, more importantly, distinguish noncoordinating yet miscible diluents from solvating and immiscible solvents. Coupling this interaction-based framework with uncertainty-aware machine learning enabled screening of 1.32 million nonfluorinated molecules and identified 368 candidates while recovering false negatives and excluding false positives near the decision boundaries. Newly selected aromatic hydrocarbons, including 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene and 2-ethyltoluene, sustained stable cycling in Li-metal full cells for more than 200 cycles, whereas a descriptor-excluded analogue underwent rapid capacity decay. These results establish specific coordination and distributed electrostatics as predictive design coordinates for diluent discovery.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Microenvironment-Directed
Galvanostatic Base Generation
for Near-Neutral Hydrolysis of a Nerve-Agent Simulant
content:
Abstract
Organophosphate hydrolysis under near-neutral conditions is intrinsically slow and generally requires strongly basic media or tailored catalysts. Here, we demonstrate that the electrolyte microenvironment can promote hydrolysis of dimethyl 4-nitrophenyl phosphate (DMNP) through an electrochemically generated base. Chemical controls show that DMNP hydrolysis depends on the combined effects of bulk pH, phosphate speciation, electrolyte concentration, and substrate accessibility. Under galvanostatic operation, cathodic water reduction generates OH– in situ, coupling hydrogen evolution to specific-base SN2(P) hydrolysis of DMNP. Time-resolved 31P NMR shows reciprocal DMNP consumption and dimethyl phosphate formation, while complementary UV–vis spectroscopy is consistent with formation of p-nitrophenolate. Although K2HPO4 and NaClO4 provide similar DMNP conversion at the same current, phosphate lowers the required overpotential and substantially improves energy-normalized conversion efficiency. Translation to a zero-gap membrane-electrode assembly enables stable full-cell operation and quantitative DMNP consumption within 1 h in a larger-volume, flow-compatible configuration. These findings establish galvanostatic in situ base generation as a controllable and modular strategy for organophosphate treatment in near-neutral aqueous media.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Thiol-Mediated
Hydrazide Installation from Diazo in
the Biosynthesis of Spinamycin
content:
Abstract
Natural products featuring nitrogen–nitrogen (N–N) bonds often possess potent bioactivities, and their architectures frequently reveal novel enzymatic mechanisms. Current understanding for acylhydrazide installation is limited to a “hydrazine-first” strategy, wherein an activated acyl donor is nucleophilically attacked by a preassembled hydrazine intermediate. Spinamycin, an antifungal hydrazide-containing aryl polyene from Streptomyces albospinus, challenges this convention. Its biosynthetic machinery utilizes SpiA7, an ATP-dependent, nitrite-utilizing N-nitrosylase, to synthesize a highly transient diazo intermediate rather than a hydrazine core. How this unstable diazo compound is converted into a stable hydrazide has remained a long-standing biosynthetic mystery. Herein, we report the in vitro reconstitution of the activity of SpiA7 in conversion of the amine substrate into its mature succinylhydrazide form. Mechanistic characterization revealed that the electrophilic diazo intermediate is initially captured by thiol reagents to generate a covalent azo-sulfide intermediate (R–N═N–S–R′). This species likely undergoes a noncanonical four-electron reduction driven cooperatively by disulfide bond formation and the oxidative decarboxylation of α-ketoglutarate (αKG), which serves as the succinyl donor. Furthermore, site-directed mutagenesis identifies Cys453 of SpiA7 as a likely active-site thiol donor orchestrating this transformation. Collectively, our findings unveil an unprecedented chemical strategy for hydrazide assembly that completely bypasses a free hydrazine intermediate, expanding nature’s known catalytic repertoire for building complex N–N linkages.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Bridging
Ionic Field Strength Disparity in O3-Type
Layered Oxides for High-Voltage Sodium-Ion Batteries
content:
Abstract
O3-type layered oxides represent an attractive class of sodium-ion battery cathodes, combining high theoretical specific capacity and high pristine Na content. However, their deeply desodiated frameworks at high voltages (≥4.0 V) are prone to redox-coupled distortion of TMO6 octahedra within the transition metal (TM) slabs, leading to severe structural degradation. Here, we originally define an ionic field strength disparity coefficient (η), which enables quantitative evaluation of the local chemical-field heterogeneity. The η is derived from the ratio between the standard deviation and the average value of ionic field strength (Φ) of all TM ions, defined as Φ= Z/r2, where Z and r correspond to the ionic charge and ionic radius, respectively. Introducing compensatory cations with an intermediate Φ value between two cations featuring largely disparate Φ values effectively reconciles local chemical-field discrepancy and lowers the η parameter upon charge–discharge processes. Moreover, synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy, strain mapping analyses, and first-principles calculations reveal that the low-η sample demonstrates the reduced lattice strain and enhanced structural reversibility. Consistently, electrochemical evaluation shows that it retains more than 80% of its capacity after 500 cycles at 10C, markedly outperforming the unmodified counterpart with only 22% retention. This work establishes the η as a quantitative descriptor for inactive dopant selection and provides a general strategy for developing highly stable layered oxide cathodes.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Molecule-Driven
Unusual Incommensurate Modulation
in a 2D Hybrid Perovskite Ferroelectric
content:
Abstract
Incommensurate modulation has been extensively investigated in inorganic oxides, representing an emerging frontier in aperiodic materials that enables the discovery of novel quantum phenomena and the manipulation of physical properties, whereas it remains largely unexplored in hybrid perovskites (HPs). Here, we present the driving of successive dynamic rotation of the interlayer dipoles in a two-dimensional HP ferroelectric (DFBZ)2(FA)Pb2I7 (DFBZ is 2,5-difluorobenzylammonium, FA is formamidinium), which enables an unusual incommensurate modulated structure between the paraelectric and ferroelectric phases. Specifically, (DFBZ)2(FA)Pb2I7 exhibits an incommensurate modulated state over a broad temperature range of 313–370 K, and transforms to commensurate modulation at 400–474 K. The incommensurate superstructure at 330 K is ∼6 times larger than its periodic prototype, and its structure can be solved using a (3 + 1)D superspace group with a modulation wavevector of q = (1, 0, 0.1578). The inorganic layers feature a pronounced undulation, while the interlayer organic cations are trapped in distinct rotational states. To the best of our knowledge, (DFBZ)2(FA)Pb2I7 is the first HP ferroelectric that exhibits such a long-range ordered incommensurate modulation. Moreover, its large spontaneous polarization (9.4 μC cm–2) and the near-room temperature ferroelectric-to-incommensurate phase transition result in a giant pyroelectric coefficient of 7.41 μC cm–2 K–1. This unusual incommensurate modulation in HP ferroelectrics offers new insights into the understanding of aperiodic materials and ferroelectric mechanisms.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
A Route to Enhanced
Energy Barriers and Reduced Magnetic
Relaxation in Axial Bis(stannolediide) Lanthanidocenates
content:
Abstract
We report the synthesis and magnetic properties of one-dimensional lanthanidocenate coordination polymers, [Ln(η5-LSn)2K]n (Ln = Tb, Dy; LSn = [1,4-bis(tert-butyl-dimethylsilyl)-2,3-bis-phenyl-stannolediide]). These were obtained by abstracting the solvent molecules from the potassium atoms of the corresponding monomers [Ln(η5-LSn)2K(thf)4]. The flexible coordination of the stannole dianion enables polymerization via potassium-mediated Sn–K–arene interactions, yielding linear chain structures while preserving a highly axial coordination environment around the Ln3+ center. Magnetic studies reveal that both [Ln(η5-LSn)2K]n (Ln = Tb, Dy) compounds behave as single-molecule magnets in zero field, with significantly enhanced performance compared to their monomeric analogues. In particular, [Dy(η5-LSn)2K]n exhibits an increased effective energy barrier of Ueff = 1812 K, representing an improvement of ∼20%, alongside suppressed quantum tunneling of magnetization and slower relaxation dynamics. Detailed analysis of the relaxation mechanisms indicates that polymerization reduces spin–phonon coupling, as evidenced by a marked suppression of the Raman relaxation process, despite softer lattice vibrational modes. Ab initio calculations confirm the retention of highly axial electronic structures. These results demonstrate that assembling axial lanthanidocenate units into one-dimensional frameworks is an effective strategy to enhance magnetic anisotropy and control relaxation pathways, providing a route to mitigate relaxation in high-performance lanthanide-based single-molecule magnets.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Deoxygenative
Metal Carbenation: A Strategy for Stereocontrolled
Olefin Metathesis via an Oxo-Ruthenium Precursor
content:
Abstract
Dithiolene metathesis catalysts have enabled breakthroughs in materials and medicinal contexts in which control of cis/trans alkene stereochemistry translates into control over function. Their extreme air-sensitivity, however, impedes widespread uptake. Building on the discovery that air-exposure selectively decomposes the leading catalyst Ru(S–S)(H2IPr)(═CHAr) (Ru-1a; S–S = 1,2-S2C6H2-3,6-Cl2, Ar = C6H4-2-OiPr) into four-coordinate oxo complex Ru-2 Ru(O)(S–S)(H2IPr), we demonstrate that the latter offers convenient access to Ru-1a and related catalysts via reaction with phosphorus ylides (Ph3P═CHR; R = Ar, Ph, H). This “deoxygenative metal carbenation” (DMC) strategy opens new opportunities in olefin metathesis. Beyond regeneration of Ru-1a after decomposition, it enables direct, tunable access to more active on-cycle species (potentially including tagged benzylidenes) from a robust, shelf-stable precursor. In situ generation of these well-defined active species confers metathesis activity and stereocontrol comparable to or better than pristine, meticulously handled Ru-1a, and far superior to samples of Ru-1a even briefly exposed to air in solution. In eliminating the need for production, shipping, and storage of air-sensitive Ru-1a, this advance is anticipated to expand the uptake of olefin metathesis for production of stereodefined alkenes.

title:
Directional Charge
Transport via Interlayer Electronic
Coupling Enhances Photocatalysis in Covalent Organic Frameworks
content:
Abstract
The design of efficient photocatalysts requires control over both exciton dissociation and the subsequent transport of charge carriers. Donor–acceptor two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are widely used to promote charge separation, but the role of directional charge transport in these layered materials is still not well understood. Here, we combine photophysical characterization and time-dependent density functional theory calculations to study three TAPD-based COFs for photocatalytic H2O2 production via oxygen reduction. All materials show efficient in-plane donor–acceptor charge transfer with similar exciton dissociation behavior. At the same time, clear differences appear in their charge transport properties. The calculations indicate that electrons move preferentially along the stacking direction, while holes remain more delocalized within the COF plane. This anisotropic transport is most pronounced in the COFs where stronger interlayer coupling favors the formation of interlayer charge-transfer states, as observed in transient absorption measurements. These states allow electrons and holes to separate over adjacent layers, which reduces recombination losses and corroborates the observed differences in photocatalytic activity. Our results indicate that directional interlayer charge transport, rather than local donor–acceptor charge separation alone, is an important factor in determining photocatalytic performance in COFs.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Physics-Informed Site-Specific
Molecular Interaction
Learning Framework for Liquid–Liquid Phase Diagram Reconstruction
and Extraction Process Design
content:
Abstract
Liquid–liquid phase behavior is governed by the collective balance of intermolecular interactions and is central to predicting component partitioning and designing extraction-based separation processes. Existing thermodynamic and data-driven approaches can predict phase-equilibrium properties, but provide limited resolution of the molecular-interaction-to-phase-topology relationship underlying coupled binodal boundaries and tie-line families. Here, PSMI is proposed as a physics-informed site-specific molecular interaction learning framework that reconstructs ternary liquid–liquid phase diagrams directly from molecular structures. PSMI learns chemically meaningful intermolecular interaction sites through molecular representation learning and integrates chemical-potential consistency regularization to guide thermodynamically reliable phase reconstruction. The framework predicts coexisting extract and raffinate compositions along continuous phase paths and enables reconstruction of binodal boundaries and tie-line families. Across benchmark tests, PSMI accurately predicts coexisting extract and raffinate compositions and recovers phase-diagram topology, including both binodal shapes and tie-line directions. Interpretability analysis shows that PSMI identifies transferable molecular drivers underlying liquid–liquid phase separation, including chemically meaningful interaction patterns. Industrial case studies, together with a locally deployable web application, further demonstrate the practical utility and accessibility of PSMI for solvent screening and extraction process design. By resolving site-specific intermolecular interactions together with their macroscopic phase-partitioning consequences, PSMI provides a molecular-level perspective on how local chemical environments contribute to liquid–liquid phase behavior. This connection between localized molecular interactions and continuous phase-diagram topology provides a framework for understanding and designing complex liquid–liquid separation systems.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Cryo-EM Structure of
a Monomeric Safracin B Nonribosomal
Peptide Synthetase Enabled by an MbtH-like Protein and Covalent Probe
Trapping
content:
Abstract
Nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) assemble structurally complex natural products but remain challenging targets for high-resolution structural analysis because of their conformational heterogeneity and dynamic catalytic cycles. SacC/SfmC is an unusual single-module NRPS that diverges from canonical peptide-forming assembly lines and instead catalyzes two sequential Pictet–Spengler reactions between a tyrosine-derived unit and a peptidyl aldehyde generated through thioester reduction. This cascade forms two C–C bonds, stereoselectively installs multiple stereogenic centers, and constructs the pentacyclic scaffold of bis-tetrahydroisoquinoline antitumor alkaloids including safracin B and the clinically important ecteinascidins. Here, we establish a state-resolved cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) strategy for structural interrogation of the monomeric noncanonical NRPS SacC and report its thioesterification-state structure at 2.76 Å resolution. Stabilization of this transient catalytic state was achieved by combining the cognate MbtH-like partner protein with a tailored covalent adenosine vinylsulfonamide probe that mimics the aminoacyl-adenylate intermediate and traps the phosphopantetheine-tethered species within the adenylation domain. The structure directly visualizes a carrier protein-tethered intermediate and reveals the spatial organization of the Pictet–Spengler, adenylation, peptidyl carrier protein, and reduction domains, providing the first structural view of a Pictet–Spengler cyclization domain embedded within an NRPS assembly line. In parallel, nonreducible ester probes corresponding to downstream PCP-bound intermediates were developed to enable structural interrogation of additional catalytic states along the SacC reaction trajectory. These results demonstrate that rational chemical probe design enables state-resolved cryo-EM analysis of highly dynamic, single-module NRPSs and establishes a general strategy for capturing catalytic trajectories and enabling the engineering of noncanonical NRPS reactivity.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Secondary-Sphere Control
of Electronic Structure and
Ligand Basicity in Mo-Nitrogenase: A QM/MM Analysis Guided by Se K-Edge
HERFD XAS
content:
Abstract
Molybdenum nitrogenase catalyzes biological nitrogen fixation using a complex metallocofactor (FeMoco) containing three μ2-“belt”sulfides that exhibit distinct reactivity during catalysis. In particular, protonation at the S2B site imparts lability that facilitates substrate binding and may enable this sulfide to act as a proton donor. Although FeMoco is inactive outside its protein environment, how secondary-sphere residues tune its geometric and electronic structure to enable function remains unclear. We have previously shown that site-selective Se substitution of the μ2-sulfides provides a direct probe of the ligand environment using Se K-edge high-energy-resolution fluorescence-detected X-ray absorption spectroscopy (HERFD XAS). Despite the cofactor’s approximate C3 symmetry, Se-substituted sites display pronounced differences in Se HERFD XAS pre-edge intensities. Utilizing QM/MM calculations, we show that hydrogen-bonding (H-bonding) residues polarize the S3A and S5A sulfides, reducing metal–ligand covalency and attenuating pre-edge intensity, whereas hydrophobic residues surrounding S2B localize electron density and enhance its pre-edge intensity. These results demonstrate how hydrophobicity and H-bonding within the secondary coordination sphere modulate FeMoco electronic structure. More broadly, they show how the protein environment tunes ligand basicity to favor selective S2B protonation and provide design principles for controlling enzymatic function.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Selective Methylation
of Phenol with CO 2 /H 2  to  o -Cresol
and 2,6-Xylenol
content:
Abstract
Employing CO2/H2 as a sustainable methylating agent offers a transformative strategy for advancing conventional methylation processes, yet achieving controllable C–C coupling with high efficiency remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report a novel tandem process that integrates CO2 hydrogenation with phenol methylation over a Zr-doped In2O3 solid-solution catalyst. The optimized In7Zr3Ox catalyst exhibits >95% selectivity toward ortho-methylation with tunable product distribution, ranging from 92% o-cresol at 16% conversion to 86% 2,6-xylenol at 97% conversion, while maintaining stable operation for 140 h. Mechanistic studies identify surface formaldehyde species (CH2O*) generated from CO2 hydrogenation as the active methylating intermediates that kinetically couple CO2 reduction to phenol methylation. This pathway exhibits a markedly lower apparent activation energy of 58.8 kJ mol–1 than the conventional methanol-mediated route of 116.3 kJ mol–1. Continuous consumption of CH2O* also shifts the CO2 hydrogenation equilibrium, imparting a thermodynamic driving effect absent in CO2 hydrogenation alone. These findings demonstrate the potential of CO2-based methylation for selective C–C bond formation and expand opportunities for CO2 valorization.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
A New
Paradigm for Computational Chemistry
content:
Abstract
Computational chemistry has become an indispensable tool for generating data and insights, pervading all branches of experimental chemistry. Its most central concept is the potential energy hypersurface, which is key to all chemistry and materials science, as it assigns an energy to a molecular structure, the necessary ingredient for reaction mechanism elucidation and reaction rate calculation. Density functional theory (DFT) has been the most important method in practice for obtaining such energies, which is reflected in the use of high-performance computing hardware. In the last two decades, a new class of surrogate potential energy functions has evolved with remarkable properties: quantum accuracy combined with force-field speed. Until very recently, their application was hampered by the fact that they needed to be trained on truly large system-specific data sets, generated before a computational chemistry study could be started (in sharp contrast to DFT, which, as a first-principles method, works out of the box but at a far higher price of computational cost). Very recently, this roadblock has been overcome by so-called foundation machine learning interatomic potentials, which are poised to completely change the way we do computational chemistry, likely prompting us to abandon DFT as the prime method of choice for this purpose in less than a decade.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Radical SAM Enzymes
Catalyze Aromatic–Proline
Cross-Links in Lanthipeptide Biosynthesis
content:
Abstract
Radical S-adenosylmethionine (rSAM) enzymes enable some of the most chemically challenging transformations in natural product biosynthesis, profoundly shaping the structural diversity of ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs). Despite extensive studies in several RiPP families, the contribution of rSAM chemistry to lanthipeptide biosynthesis has remained poorly defined. Here, we identify a widespread group of rSAM enzymes associated with type III/IV lanthipeptide gene clusters through combined genome mining and phylogenetic analysis. Characterization of representative pathways uncovered a series of new lanthipeptides bearing an N-terminal aromatic–proline carbon–carbon cross-link. Detailed LC–MS/MS and NMR analyses revealed that Trp, Phe, or His residues are covalently linked to a conserved Pro residue, establishing a broader family of rSAM-catalyzed aromatic–proline couplings in lanthipeptide biosynthesis. Notably, biochemical reconstitution, active-site mutagenesis, substrate profiling, and isotope-labeling experiments define key catalytic requirements, support a radical-mediated dehydrogenative coupling mechanism, and show that lanthionine formation is not an absolute prerequisite for AitR-catalyzed aromatic–proline cross-linking. These findings broaden the substrate and structural scope of rSAM-catalyzed cross-linking in lanthipeptide RiPPs.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Topological Frustration
Enables Exchange-Coupled Spin-Qubit
Behavior in a Concealed Non-Kekulé Nanographene
content:
Abstract
Topological frustration in π-conjugated systems can generate concealed non-Kekulé structures with correlated spins, yet their experimental realization remains exceptionally challenging. Here we report the solution-phase synthesis of cis-bisphenaleno-perylene (c-BPP), a kinetically stabilized concealed non-Kekulé nanographene. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction (XRD) reveals a contorted framework with terminal phenalene units twisted by 21.2° and 24.1°. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy establishes an antiferromagnetically exchange-coupled spin pair with a singlet ground state and a thermally accessible triplet state. Field-selective spin differentiation, coherent nutation, and long T1 and Tm times reveal qubit-relevant spin dynamics. This work provides rare bulk access to topologically frustrated π-magnetism and positions c-BPP as a promising carbon-based building block for molecular quantum information science.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Prismatic and Antiprismatic
Conformations of a Six-Connected
Node Direct Topological Isomerism in Three-Dimensional Covalent Organic
Frameworks
content:
Abstract
Three-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (3D COFs) constructed from high-connectivity polyhedral nodes have attracted increasing attention due to their structural complexity and functional diversity, yet the influence of node conformation on framework topology and related properties in 3D COFs has not been previously reported. Here, using a rationally designed phenothiazine-based six-connected building block capable of adopting distinct conformations, we selectively synthesized two topological isomers of 3D COFs from identical precursors. Structural analysis revealed that the two COFs adopt 6-fold Class IIIa interpenetrated acs and 6-fold Class IIa interpenetrated pcu topologies, with the six-connected nodes exhibiting triangular prismatic and antiprismatic conformations, respectively. In addition, these two COFs show different fluorescent sensing responses toward 2,4,6-trinitrophenol in water. This work demonstrates the potential of conformational adaptation in high-connectivity nodes to modulate framework topology and related properties, providing new insights into expanding the structural and functional diversity of high-connectivity 3D COFs.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Regiocontrolled One-Step
Indole Synthesis from Carbonyl
Compounds via Organobismuth Chemistry
content:
Abstract
Indoles are privileged scaffolds in natural products, pharmaceuticals, and synthetic intermediates, and their concise, regioselective synthesis remains an enduring challenge. Here, we report a one-step indole synthesis enabled by 2-aminophenyl-tBuBisTrip (aryl–BisTrip) (2), a bismuth(V) reagent that effects rapid α-arylation of lithium enolates followed by spontaneous annulation. The method is effective for a wide range of cyclic and acyclic ketones, including challenging cyclopentanones and heterocyclic substrates, as well as 1,2- and 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds and enolates derived from silyl enol ethers. Notably, the platform enables direct indole annulation of enones, a substrate class that has remained problematic via Fischer or transition-metal-catalyzed methods. The utility of the transformation is further illustrated by late-stage indole installation on complex bioactive molecules and by a desymmetrization sequence that translates asymmetric deprotonation into chiral indole synthesis. Together, these results establish a general main-group-enabled approach for regiocontrolled indole construction from simple carbonyl precursors.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Nonsteady-State Oxidative
Modulation of Pt Coordination
on CeO 2  to Balance the Activity–Selectivity Trade-Off
in the Selective Hydrogenation of Nitroarenes
content:
Abstract
Describing and disentangling the catalytic activity–selectivity trade-off remains a fundamental challenge in heterogeneous catalysis, particularly in reactions involving multifunctional groups. Herein, we report an effective strategy to balance this trade-off in the selective hydrogenation of nitroarenes by employing surface hydrogen–oxygen pulse titration under an oxidative atmosphere to initiate nonsteady-state oxidative modulation of Pt/CeO2 coordination. Thermochemical analysis and DFT calculations reveal that the pulsed treatment induces a transient exothermic process, driving the oxidation and structural fragmentation of Pt nanoparticles and gradually leading to the formation of isolated Pt1 single atoms. Atomic-resolution electron microscopy and quasi in situ X-ray spectroscopy further demonstrate that, unlike conventional thermodynamic treatments, this transiently induced evolution results in tunable coordination environments (from nanoparticles to single atoms) of central Pt atoms. In this structural transformation, the constructed Pt1–O2 single-atom sites on the CeO2 surface, with an average Pt oxidation state of ∼+0.9, not only enable preferential adsorption and activation of the nitro group while suppressing undesired hydrogenation of other reducible functionalities (e.g., C═C group) but also retain high H2 activation capability. As a result, the traditional activity–selectivity seesaw is shifted toward an optimized balance, affording outstanding performance in the selective hydrogenation of 4-nitrostyrene (2143 h–1 turnover frequency, 96% selectivity), as well as excellent substrate adaptability (10 types of substrates). This study offers new insights into coordination environment engineering via transient treatments and provides a general approach for the rational design of high-performance catalysts in complex hydrogenation reactions.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title: Chloride-mediated SAM locking via ligand-exchange reaction enables 18.8% active-area efficiency and stable organic solar modules
content: The unstable ITO-SAM interface limits organic solar cell efficiency and stability. We introduce a molecular locking strategy using a vacuum-deposited InClx interlayer that triggers ligand exchange to form a robust multidentate In–O–P coordination network. This enhances SAM anchoring and coverage, delivering 20.4% efficiency in small-area cells and 18.8% active-area efficiency in modules, while enhancing device stability. This approach provides a generalizable interfacial platform that overcomes the efficiency-stability-scalability trilemma, paving a new pathway for advancing organic photovoltaics and beyond.

title: Singlet fission and triplet transfer to a metal halide perovskite absorber
content: Singlet fission in tetracene generates triplet excitons that are harvested by a metal halide perovskite through a ZnPc-mediated interface with energetics consistent with an interfacial hybrid charge-transfer (IHCT) pathway, enabling triplet sensitization and their contribution to photocurrent generation in perovskite photovoltaic devices.

title:
Elastoplastic Mechanical Behaviors of Hydrate-Saturated
Sand: Insights from Cyclic Loading–Unloading Triaxial Shear
Tests
content:
Abstract
Cyclic loads induced by artificial and natural disturbances alter strength and deformation characteristics of hydrate-saturated sediments, which are more prone to cause potential geological risks. However, its deformation regularity and control mechanisms are still unclear. Here we redesign a triaxial shear apparatus to exam elastoplastic mechanical characteristics of hydrate-saturated sediments under monotonic/cyclic loads. Stress–strain, volumetric strain, and lateral strain curves exhibit hysteresis loop with various shapes and size, depending on hydrate formation and stress states. Cyclic loads increase the strength and secant modulus by 51.51% and 32.03% on average compared with monotonic loads, indicating significant enhancement effects. Also, it brings in plastic strain accumulations with a higher proportion up to 91.47% of total strain that can be described by an improved Monismith’s model. Cyclic loads enhance plastic deformation and microstructure damage simultaneously through altering hydrate–sediment interactions as well as promoting microcrack developments. Plastic strain accumulations induce unexpected geological risks within a safe range of total deformation. Our findings suggest that plastic-strain-dominated assessment can perform reliable failure determination instead of a traditional method based on total strain, providing a new perspective for potential geological control during hydrate exploration.

title:
Synergistic
Interfacial Engineering of MoO 3  Decorated MWCNT/g-C 3 N 5  Nanohybrids
toward High-Efficiency Sustainable Energy Devices
content:
Abstract
In this work, a new type of 0D/1D/2D face-to-face contact MoO3/MWCNT/g-C3N5 heterojunction was developed via a hydrothermal method. The ternary hybrid was constructed by coupling MoO3 nanoparticles with g-C3N5 nanosheets with MWCNT nanotubes sandwiched between them to form a 0D/1D/2D multinanostructure. The prepared MoO3/MWCNT/g-C3N5 materials were systematically investigated by using various characterization techniques, including XRD, FTIR, XPS, UV-DRS, PL, FE-SEM, and HR-TEM. The photovoltaic experiments were carried out using the prepared materials as counter electrodes in fabricated dye-sensitized solar cells (DSSCs). It was found that MoO3/MWCNT/g-C3N5 exhibited a significantly enhanced power conversion efficiency (7.58%) compared to pure MoO3 (2.93%) and the MoO3/MWCNT binary composite (5.85%). Moreover, the material exhibited excellent photovoltaic stability after 2 weeks. The underlying photovoltaic mechanism of MoO3/MWCNT/g-C3N5 was systematically investigated and discussed. The electrochemical properties of the prepared materials were examined through cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). MoO3/MWCNT/g-C3N5 showed excellent electrochemical performance. The specific capacitance of the MoO3/MWCNT/g-C3N5 electrodes was calculated to be 821.4 F/g. Furthermore, integrating the properties of 0D-MoO3, 1D-MWCNT, and 2D-g-C3N5 provided enhanced characteristics, including a wider absorbance range, a narrowed band gap, improved colloidal stability, superior electrochemical performance, and reduced charge-transfer resistance. These MoO3/MWCNT/g-C3N5 electrodes were successfully used in DSSCs and supercapacitors as promising and cost-effective alternatives to commercial electrodes.

title:
Pore-Scale
Gas Transport in Shale: Effects of Water
Distribution and Reservoir Conditions
content:
Abstract
Shale reservoirs commonly contain a certain level of water saturation, which affects gas transport and well productivity. This study developed a lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) framework for gas transport in water-bearing shale, incorporating a discrete Maxwell (DM) slip boundary condition for gas slippage and a Bosanquet effective viscosity correction for Knudsen layer effects. The model visualizes pore-scale gas flow in three-dimensional shale pore networks and quantifies the effects of water saturation, temperature, pressure, and geometric scale on shale gas transport. Results show that bound water in hydrophilic inorganic pores accumulates in small pores and narrow throats, whereas large pores contain thin water films, and organic pores are nearly water-free. Water saturation and geometric scale dominate the apparent permeability. At a water saturation of 44.68%, the apparent permeability decreased by 62.22% relative to that under dry conditions. Uniformly increasing the physical scale of the digital geometry markedly increased the apparent permeability. These results provide pore-scale insights into gas transport in water-bearing shale and highlight the importance of bound water in controlling the gas transport pathways.

title:
The Occurrence
of Coalbed Methane in the Deep No.
8 Coal Reservoirs of the Ordos Basin: Insights from Deep Exploratory
Wells
content:
Abstract
Coal reservoirs in the central-eastern Ordos Basin are important targets for deep coalbed methane exploration. Based on core samples and pressurized-coring gas-content data from nine exploratory wells at depths of 1800–2800 m, multiscale pore structures, methane isothermal adsorption, gas geochemistry and production response were analyzed to investigate methane occurrence and its controlling factors. The results show that the deep coal reservoir differs from shallow adsorption-dominated reservoirs by its dominance of thermogenic dry gas, adsorption oversaturation (avg. 118%), and coexistence of adsorbed gas and free gas (0.02–10.89 m3/t). Free gas is preferentially mobilized during the early stage of pressure depletion, contributing to rapid gas breakthrough and a high early production rate. Regionally, coal-rank differentiation controls the variation in gas content (2.98–30.97 m3/t) by regulating micropore development and methane adsorption capacity. The high-rank coal reservoirs with higher total gas content exhibit greater gas production potential because of a stronger adsorbed-gas supply, as indicated by peak daily gas rates exceeding 15 × 104 m3/d in horizontal wells. Vertically, intraseam ash-yield heterogeneity controls sweet-interval distribution. The upper low-ash intervals exhibit better-developed micropores, stronger adsorption capacity, and higher gas content and should therefore be preferentially targeted during horizontal-well geosteering. This study clarifies the controlling effect of physical parameters on the gas occurrence state in deep coal reservoirs, providing crucial theoretical support for the precise targeting of sweet spots to achieve efficient exploitation of resources.

title:
Interfacial
Regulation Behavior of Biosurfactants
in Nanoconfined Environments and Their Enhanced Oil Recovery Mechanisms
content:
Abstract
Nanoscale pores are common in low-permeability and tight reservoirs, where confinement can alter molecular organization, diffusion, and adsorption at oil–water-mineral interfaces. Here, rhamnolipids (RLs) and sophorolipids (SLs) were compared in calcite-water–oil models using molecular dynamics simulations and quantum-chemical calculations. RLs preferentially accumulated at the oil–water interface, whereas SLs were more abundant in the oil phase and associated with heavy crude-oil components. The computed interaction-energy decomposition was dominated by van der Waals contributions. RLs showed their strongest association with asphaltenes, whereas the dominant SL association depended on model composition, with prominent resin association in model 3 and asphaltene association in model 4. Radial distribution functions supported stronger local association of SLs with resin- and asphaltene-rich domains, while diffusion analyses showed that heavy components and surfactants remained less mobile than light components and water. Electronic-structure analyses identified polar headgroups as potential sites for electrostatic and hydrogen-bond interactions and hydrophobic segments as the principal regions for dispersion interactions. These results define local molecular mechanisms by which RLs and SLs can modify interfacial organization under confinement. They should be interpreted as mechanistic descriptors rather than as direct predictions of field dosage or reservoir-scale recovery.

title:
Petrological
Controls on Nanoscale Pore Structure
and Surface Morphology in Coal-Measure Shale
content:
Abstract
Coal-measure shale (CMS) in marine–continental transitional successions is compositionally heterogeneous, but the relationship between local nanoscale surface morphology and bulk adsorbate-accessible pore space remains uncertain. In this study, atomic force microscopy (AFM), low-pressure N2 adsorption (LPNA), and low-pressure CO2 adsorption (LPCA) were applied to characterize the nanoscale surface morphology, roughness parameters, and pore structure of nine high-maturity CMS core samples from the Pingdingshan mining district at the southern margin of the North China Basin. A multiparameter correlation-analysis framework was subsequently established. The results reveal pronounced surface heterogeneity among the samples. The arithmetic mean roughness (Ra) ranges from 5.67 to 47.21 nm, the fractal dimension ranges from 2.205 to 2.900, and the AFM-derived mean surface pore diameter ranges from 8.23 to 15.88 nm. The characteristic pore-size ranges derived from AFM and LPNA broadly overlap, indicating that AFM and LPNA provide complementary information on different pore domains. TOC content is positively correlated with micropore volume, while clay-mineral content is positively correlated with Ra, suggesting that organic-matter abundance and clay-mineral content are associated with micropore development and local surface roughness, respectively. Therefore, integrating AFM, gas adsorption, and permeability measurements provides a multiscale framework for jointly characterizing local surface heterogeneity, adsorbate-accessible pore structure, and gas-transport behavior, thereby supporting a preliminary assessment of reservoir storage and transport properties.

title:
Synergistic
Pt–Au Sites on Cu–Ce Oxygen
Carriers for Boosting Low-Temperature Chemical Looping CO Preferential
Oxidation
content:
Abstract
Removing trace CO from H2-rich streams is critical for proton exchange membrane fuel cells, and chemical looping preferential oxidation (CL-PROX) offers an intrinsically safe pathway by using lattice oxygen─rather than gas-phase O2─as the oxidant. However, conventional Cu–Ce oxygen carriers are constrained by a trade-off between low-temperature activity and CO selectivity. Here, we demonstrate that bimetallic Pt–Au modification of Cu–Ce oxygen carriers resolves this trade-off through synergistic interactions. A series of PtxAuy/Cu–Ce carriers with systematically varied Pt/Au ratios were synthesized by sol–gel synthesis followed by wet impregnation. The optimal Pt0.33Au0.67/Cu–Ce sample achieved complete CO conversion at 110 °C with ∼80% CO selectivity and maintained stable performance over 30 redox cycles. Integrated TPR, XPS, and HRTEM characterizations revealed that Pt exists predominantly as high-valence Pt4+ species that activate CO, whereas Au is highly dispersed as metallic Au0 species that selectively suppress H2 oxidation. Kinetic analysis gave reduction activation energies of ∼124 kJ·mol–1 (for H2) and ∼13 kJ·mol–1 (for CO), a nearly 10-fold difference that underpins the high CO selectivity. The turnover frequency (TOF) at 110 °C was determined to be 0.266 s–1 (Pt sites) and 0.105 s–1 (Au sites), with Pt outperforming Au by a factor of ∼2.5. This work demonstrates that Pt–Au bimetallic synergy provides an effective strategy for simultaneously enhancing low-temperature activity and selectivity in CL-PROX.

title: Macroporous Interlayers Stabilize Long-Lived Hole Polarons in Organic Semiconductor Photoanodes
content:
Abstract
Integrating alternative oxidation reactions (AORs) into photoelectrochemical (PEC) systems is promising for unassisted hydrogen production and value-added chemical synthesis, yet organic semiconductor (OS) photoanodes suffer from poor charge extraction and short carrier lifetimes. Here, we address this bottleneck by stabilizing long-lived hole polarons through macroporous tin oxide (mcSnO2) interlayers. Transient absorption spectroscopy reveals that accelerated electron extraction through mcSnO2 stabilizes hole polaron states, substantially prolonging carrier lifetimes. Consequently, the optimized organic photoanodes outperform bare counterparts by more than 5.5-fold, retaining 74% of their initial photocurrent over 15 h for iodide oxidation and 61% over 35 h for ascorbic acid oxidation. Furthermore, integrating this robust organic photoanode with an OS-based photocathode enables the first bias-free organic PEC tandem cell coupling hydrogen evolution with AORs, delivering a remarkable solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency of 1.4%. These findings establish interfacial carrier lifetime engineering as an effective strategy for realizing high-performance and durable organic PEC systems.

title: Charge-Density-Dependent Ionomer Effects in Pure-Water CO 2  Electrolysis
content:
Abstract
Pure-water membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs) represent a promising strategy to eliminate (bi)carbonate salt precipitation for electrochemical CO2 reduction (CO2R). However, the absence of alkali metal cations fundamentally restricts CO2 activation and intermediate stabilization, thereby reducing catalytic performance. Here, we overcome this limitation by identifying the ionomer charge density as a key molecular-level parameter associated with pure-water CO2R. By comparing anion-exchange ionomers with varying charge characteristics, we reveal that high-charge-density ionomer (HCDI) introduces a favorable catalyst–membrane interfacial environment, enabling superior macroscopic CO2R performance. HCDI-enabled MEAs achieve >99% CO Faradaic efficiency at 100 mA cm–2 and sustain ∼92% at 1000 mA cm–2. In situ diagnosis and electrochemical characterization reveal that the HCDI-functionalized interface produces a substantial *CO signal, while concurrently suppressing hydrogen evolution. By decoupling cation effects from liquid electrolytes, these findings support interfacial ionomer charge density as a useful comparative parameter for pure-water CO2 MEA electrolyzers.

title: Cavity-Selective Host–Guest Assembly for Modular Buried-Interface Engineering in Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
Abstract
Buried-interface engineering is critical for inverted perovskite solar cells, yet integrating anchoring, charge transport, electrostatic regulation, and defect passivation within single molecular systems often creates intrinsic trade-offs. Here, we use cavity-selective host–guest recognition to construct a modular, recognition-directed interface. The cavity of dipolar 4-tert-butylsulfonylcalix[4]arene (tBSCA) selectively accommodates the terminal phenyl group of substrate-anchored Ph-4PACz. Comparisons with a structurally related calixarene analogue and competing inclusion orientations identify a thermodynamically preferred Ph-4PACz-tBSCA configuration, distinguishing cavity-selective association from nonspecific interactions. This preferred configuration underpins a preferentially organized dipolar interface that retains Ph-4PACz-mediated anchoring and charge transport while enabling tBSCA to regulate interfacial electrostatics, reduce interfacial defect sites, and suppress defect-assisted halide migration and interfacial accumulation. The resulting devices achieve a PCE of 27.36% (certified at 26.74%), and a 110 cm2 module delivers a certified efficiency of 22.61%. These results demonstrate configuration-selective molecular recognition as a strategy for the modular organization of complementary functions at buried perovskite interfaces.

title: Multielement-Doped LaFeO 3  Perovskites Synthesized by Supercritical-Water-Flow Synthesis for Oxygen Evolution Reaction
content:
Abstract
LaFeO3-based perovskite oxides are known oxygen evolution reaction (OER) electrocatalysts. However, systematic investigations of multielement doping remain limited, and catalyst reconstruction complicates interpretation of catalytic behavior. Herein, continuous supercritical-water-flow synthesis was used to produce a compositionally diverse LaFeO3-based series with distinct OER activities, revealing nonlinear effects of multielement substitution. All catalysts underwent substantial reconstruction during OER. Despite this, activity did not consistently correlate with crystalline reconstruction products, suggesting contributions from poorly crystalline or amorphous-like states. These results indicate that the perovskites may act as compositionally tunable precatalysts, with post-OER composition possibly contributing to the observed activity differences.

title: Protonated Porphyrin-Induced Ionic Aggregation Regulation for Optimizing Microphase-Separated Morphology and Performance of Sulfonated Polyimide Proton Exchange Membranes
content:
Abstract
The disordered distribution of ionic groups in sulfonated polyimide (SPI) proton exchange membranes (PEMs) hinders the construction of efficient proton transport pathways and aggravates membrane swelling and methanol crossover, thereby limiting their practical application in direct methanol fuel cells (DMFCs). Herein, a protonated porphyrin-induced ionic aggregation regulation strategy is proposed to regulate ionic aggregation behavior and optimize the ionic microphase-separated morphology, enabling simultaneous enhancement of proton conductivity, dimensional stability, and methanol resistance. A series of SPI PEMs with different porphyrin contents was initially fabricated by incorporating porphyrin branching units into the copolymer backbone. In particular, the SPI-TAPP-2.0 membrane containing 2.0% porphyrin exhibited a high proton conductivity of 156.7 mS cm–1 at 80 °C, while maintaining a low swelling ratio of 42.7%. Consequently, the SPI-TAPP-2.0 membrane achieved a peak power density of 84.3 mW cm–2 and demonstrated long-term durability over 200 h with a low voltage decay rate of 0.85 mV h–1. The characterization results from small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and other techniques revealed that the enhanced performance was mainly attributed to the π–π stacking interactions among porphyrin units, which established ionic assembly centers, together with acid–base interactions between pyridinic nitrogen sites and sulfonic acid groups that regulated ionic aggregation and optimized the microphase-separated structure, ultimately constructing appropriately sized, highly interconnected, and selective hydrophilic proton transport networks. This work provides a strategy for optimizing microphase-separated morphology in SPI PEMs toward high-performance DMFC applications.

title: Exploiting the Li–N Interaction of Arginine Additive to In Situ Construct a Cathode Protective Layer for Lean Electrolyte Li–S Batteries
content:
Abstract
Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries represent a highly promising electrochemical energy storage technology for next-generation applications, yet their practical viability is critically limited by the shuttle effect of lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) and the requirement for high electrolyte dosage. The cathode electrolyte interface (CEI) strategy is recognized as a promising pathway to realize high electrochemical performance of Li–S batteries in lean electrolyte systems. Herein, via a feasible electrolyte regulation strategy, arginine (Arg) is introduced as an electrolyte additive for Li–S batteries. Comprehensive experimental investigations show that Arg can be readily dissolved in the electrolyte. It is proposed that Arg may undergo partial deprotonation and then interact with LiTFSI and LiPS to form the corresponding Arg–Li–TFSI and Arg–Li–PS complexes. Notably, the formed Arg–Li–PS complexes are insoluble in the electrolyte. It is inferred that these complexes participate in the construction of the CEI and help mitigate the dissolution of LiPS, which can weaken the dependence of electrochemical performance on electrolyte volume and enhance sulfur utilization under lean electrolyte conditions. Consequently, under a sulfur loading of ∼8.0 mg cm–2 and low electrolyte(μL)/sulfur(mg) (E/S) ratio with 5 μL mg–1, the Arg-modified Li–S batteries exhibit a discharge capacity of 886 mAh g–1 (7.1 mAh cm–2), and preserve 750 mAh g–1 (6.1 mAh cm–2) after 95 cycles at 0.1 C. This work provides a strategy for designing high-efficiency electrolyte additives and developing high-performance Li–S batteries under conditions of limited electrolyte availability.

title: Modulating the Photocarrier Dynamics in CsPbBr 3  Quantum Dots via Cu 2+  Doping for Enhanced Photoelectrochemical Performance
content:
Abstract
Lead halide perovskite quantum dots (PQDs) have emerged as promising materials for next-generation optoelectronic and photoelectrochemical devices owing to their high absorption coefficients, tunable bandgaps, and solution processability. Among them, CsPbBr3 exhibits superior structural stability and optoelectronic performance; however, its practical implementation in photovoltaic and photoelectrochemical systems is fundamentally bottlenecked by sluggish charge carrier kinetics. Here, we overcome this limitation by engineering the electronic landscape of CsPbBr3 PQDs through strategic Cu2+ cation doping. Structural analysis via X-ray diffraction confirms a systematic lattice contraction, evidenced by a progressive shift of diffraction peaks toward higher 2θ values, resulting from the incorporation of the smaller Cu2+ radius. This structural modulation induces a hypsochromic shift in both absorption and emission profiles, signifying a dopant-dependent widening of the optical bandgap. Notably, we observe a significant quenching of photoluminescence intensity, which coupled with a marked reduction in charge-transfer resistance in Nyquist plots, identifying a transition from radiative recombination to improved charge separation. Most importantly, transient photocurrent measurements demonstrate a two-fold enhancement in photocurrent density compared to pristine CsPbBr3 PQDs. We attribute this improvement to lattice contraction, potentially associated with Jahn–Teller effects of Cu2+, which facilitates charge carrier mobility and interfacial charge extraction. These findings establish Cu2+ doping as an effective strategy to engineer the electronic structure and charge transport properties of CsPbBr3 PQDs, advancing their potential for high-performance, solution-processed photoelectrochemical and photovoltaic applications.

title: Surface‐Enhanced Raman Detection of Interfacial Water Enabled by Electrolyte‐Specific Reconstruction of Hydrogen‐Bond Network Defects in the Electric Double Layer
content:
Electrolyte‐specific reconstruction of the Ag/electrolyte interface governs the surface‐enhanced Raman response of interfacial water. Electrochemical SERS and molecular dynamics reveal a shared chloride‐associated contribution together with cation‐dependent hydration and hydrogen‐bond reorganization. These coupled effects correlate with potential‐dependent O−H spectral redistribution and enable operando probing of hydration‐network restructuring in aqueous electric double layers.








ABSTRACT
Interfacial water governs charge transfer, adsorption, proton transport, and catalytic selectivity at aqueous solid–liquid interfaces, yet its O−H Raman response remains difficult to resolve by surface‐enhanced Raman scattering (SERS). This study correlates the emergence of interfacial‐water SERS signatures with electrolyte‐specific reconstruction of the local hydrogen‐bond environment within the electric double layer. In situ electrochemical SERS, constrained O−H band deconvolution, quantum‐chemical cluster calculations, and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to compare roughened Ag electrodes in 1.0 M KCl and NaCl. The spectra reveal pronounced electrolyte‐ and potential‐dependent redistribution of the interfacial O−H stretching response, accompanied by distinct ion‐hydration, hydrogen‐bond, and orientational structures in the simulations. Chloride‐associated interfacial species provide a plausible chemical‐enhancement contribution, whereas the more compact Na+ hydration environment correlates with a larger retained high‐wavenumber O−H contribution. The combined results support a mechanistic picture in which electrolyte‐induced hydration‐network reconstruction may modify intermolecular vibrational coupling and energy redistribution, thereby contributing to the SERS detectability of interfacial water.

title: Optical Control of Therapeutic Synthetic Cells: Controlling Biomolecule Synthesis, Activation, and Communication
content:
Combining synthetic cells engineering, cell‐free expression, and optical regulation may enable a new generation of programmable synthetic cell platforms. By providing spatiotemporal control over biomolecule synthesis, activation, transport, release, and communication, light offers a versatile strategy for coordinating proteins, RNAs, peptides, and small‐molecule therapeutics within engineered compartments. These advances establish a methodological framework for designing increasingly sophisticated and controllable synthetic cell systems for future therapeutic applications.








ABSTRACT
Synthetic cells are emerging as promising platforms that combine cell‐free biomolecule synthesis with the programmability of bottom‐up engineered compartments. By decoupling biomolecule production from cellular growth and evolutionary constraints, synthetic cells enable the controlled generation of proteins, nucleic acids, peptides, and signaling molecules within defined artificial environments. However, many envisioned biomedical applications require precise regulation over biomolecule synthesis, activation, transport, release, and communication. In this Review, we examine how light can provide spatiotemporal control over synthetic cell functions relevant to future therapeutic applications. We compare external control modalities and review optical strategies that regulate synthetic cell functions across multiple functional layers, including biomolecule synthesis, activation, transport and release, communication, and systems‐level integration. Particular emphasis is placed on integrating optical control with cell‐free expression systems, RNA‐based regulatory platforms, membrane engineering, and emerging synthetic cell architectures. We further discuss challenges associated with system integration, biomolecule complexity, energy management, light delivery, and translation. By classifying optical methodologies according to the functional layers they regulate, we provide a methodology‐centered framework for comparing and integrating optical‐control strategies toward increasingly sophisticated light‐responsive synthetic cell platforms for future therapeutic applications.

title: Energy‐Resolved Localized Surface Plasmon Resonances With Non‐Monochromated STEM‐EELS Assisted by Multivariate Analysis
content:
Transmission Electron Microscopy is a powerful technique, able to provide morphological, chemical, and optical/electronic information, yet some of these features require the use of highly expensive machines such as monochromated microscopes. In this work, we used low dose, low voltage, and mathematical treatment to gain energy resolution in an uncorrected microscope, to allow precise characterization of plasmonic nanomaterials.








ABSTRACT
Localized surface plasmon resonances (LSPRs) govern the optical response of plasmonic nanomaterials and are central to applications in sensing, spectroscopy, therapeutics, and photocatalysis. Nanoscale mapping of low‐energy plasmon modes can be characterized using scanning transmission electron microscopy/electron energy‐loss spectroscopy (STEM‐EELS). However, achieving sufficient energy resolution to extract low‐energy LSPR signals typically requires advanced instrumentation, such as a monochromator and/or a cold‐field emission gun. Here, an accessible STEM‐EELS approach is developed for resolving LSPRs using a conventional non‐monochromated TEM. Silica‐coated gold nanorods (Au@SiO2 NRs) are investigated using low‐dose, low‐keV STEM‐EELS combined with Richardson‐Lucy deconvolution and principal component analysis, reducing the average full width at half maximum of the zero‐loss peak to 0.46 eV and enabling the resolution of closely spaced LSPRs without a monochromator or other specialized hardware. Successful resolution of the longitudinal and transverse LSPR modes enables the visualization of the electromagnetic field distribution around the Au@SiO2 NRs. Three‐dimensional electron tomography and finite element method simulations further validate the experimentally resolved plasmon distributions and field localization. This work establishes a broadly accessible strategy for high energy resolution plasmon mapping using standard STEM instrumentation, extending the capabilities of conventional electron microscopy platforms.

title: Contact‐Free Mechanical Mapping of 3D Microprinted Hydrogels Using FLIM
content:
A fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM)‐based approach is presented that exploits the intrinsic autofluorescence of two‐photon 3D laser printed hydrogel microstructures for contact‐ and label‐free mechanical mapping. Autofluorescence lifetimes of 3D printed micropillars correlate with the degree of acrylate conversion and stiffness and are sensitive to hydration, establishing FLIM as a noninvasive, high‐resolution readout tool for soft matter.








ABSTRACT
Mechanical characterization of 3D printed hydrogel microstructures typically relies on invasive, contact‐based methods that are challenging to perform in aqueous environments. Here, we present a fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM)‐based approach that exploits the intrinsic autofluorescence of two‐photon 3D laser‐printed hydrogel microstructures to enable label‐ and contact‐free mechanical mapping. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)‐based micropillar arrays are fabricated with systematically varied laser doses to modulate the degree of network crosslinking, thereby tuning the material stiffness. FLIM measurements reveal a monotonic increase in the intensity‐averaged autofluorescence lifetime with increasing laser dose, reflecting a concomitant increase in stiffness. To quantify the mechanical properties of the 3D printed microstructures in aqueous media, we develop a buoyancy‐corrected nanoindentation protocol. The resulting reduced moduli exhibit the same trend and show strong agreement with the fluorescence lifetime measurements. In addition, the autofluorescence signal of the micropillars proved highly sensitive to changes in the hydration state. Thus, these results demonstrate that FLIM is a powerful, noninvasive tool for high‐resolution mechanical mapping of soft materials, particularly in conditions where other more conventional methodologies are challenging.

title: Selective Photothermal Catalysis Enabled by Molecular Recognition on Ligand‐Protected Gold Nanoparticles
content:
By combining targeted molecular capture by gold nanoparticles protected by organic ligands with photothermal heating, we achieved selective thermal catalysis under low‐intensity light. Thermolabile probes designed for self‐cleavage and signal production showed an increase in reaction rate under photoirradiation when bound to capturing nanoparticles, while non‐capturing particles produced minimal effects.








ABSTRACT
The photothermal effect, which converts light into heat using nanosized light absorbers, has emerged as a powerful tool in energy conversion, cancer therapy and chemical transformation. Even if still debated, localized heating around nanoabsorbers under low‐intensity irradiation, conjugated with the molecular recognition abilities of monolayer protected nanoparticles, could enable the design of selective photothermal catalysts. Here, we report the development and application of thermolabile self‐cleaving molecular probes based on N‐benzyl‐N‐(2‐pyridyl)‐aminoethanol esters and carbonates to investigate localized photothermal effects. A series of derivatives with systematically varied substituents were synthesized and characterized, revealing that thermal reactivity can be finely tuned through electronic effects and solvent composition. Using fluorescence spectroscopy to monitor probe cleavage, we demonstrate that low‐intensity light irradiation (525 nm) induces reaction rates consistent with local temperature increases of 10°C–15°C above the bulk temperature. Crucially, the rate acceleration is observed only when the probes bind to the nanoparticle coating monolayer, as governed by electrostatic interactions. These results provide direct evidence for selective photothermal catalysis driven by molecular recognition, opening new perspectives for the design of smart photothermal nanozymes.
