title:
MetaTag: A Biochemical
Reaction-Guided Design Strategy
for New Metabolite Discovery
content:
Abstract
Most small-molecule features detected in untargeted metabolomics remain unannotated, representing the dark matter of the metabolome. Here, we introduce MetaTag, a biochemical-reaction-guided framework that generates high-probability novel metabolites by combining abundant endogenous metabolites with common enzymatic transformations derived from KEGG pathways. In this proof-of-concept implementation, we focused on N-acylation and N-alkylation reactions. We synthesized and characterized a physical library of 1068 compounds, creating a public MS/MS database (https://mtdb-website.vercel.app). Screening against 27 rat tissues matched 180 previously unreported metabolites with 6 at level 1 (confirmed by RT, formula, MS/MS) and 174 at level 2 (confirmed by RT, formula). These metabolites exhibited tissue-specific distributions and participated in the interorgan exchange during fasting. Functional interrogation of one such metabolite, N-propionyltaurine, demonstrated its role as a redox-sensitive regulator in brown adipocytes. This biochemistry-guided strategy provides a scalable platform for the discovery of previously uncharacterized bioactive metabolites.

title:
Hybrid Solid Oxide
Cell Enables Efficient and Robust
High-Temperature CO 2  Electrolysis
content:
Abstract
Electrocatalytic conversion of CO2 into chemicals and fuels offers a promising route toward a circular carbon economy. High-temperature CO2 electroreduction in solid oxide electrolysis cells (SOECs) delivers high selectivity and energy efficiency, but balancing mechanical robustness and electrochemical performance remains challenging. Here, we address this challenge by introducing a hybrid ionic-conductor architecture that spatially decouples electrocatalysis, ionic transport, and mechanical support into function-specific layers. The resulting cell combines high mechanical robustness (fracture load > 7 N) with 1.5–3.0-fold higher CO2-to-CO activity than state-of-the-art SOECs over 600–800 °C. Stable operation is maintained for over 1000 h at 1.0 A cm–2. Furthermore, we demonstrate scalability with a single-cell area of 100 cm2, achieving total currents up to 120 A and powers up to 200 W. This work establishes an effective strategy for developing mechanically resilient, efficient, and scalable energy conversion devices.

title:
Finding the Sweet Spot:
Isomerization Strategy Enables
Balanced Energy Dissipation of NIR-II AIEgens for “One-for-All”
Tumor Phototheranostics
content:
Abstract
“One-for-all” phototheranostics with the second near-infrared window (NIR-II) emission have garnered great enthusiasm for seamlessly integrating superb imaging and high-efficiency therapy into a single formula. However, it is still a nontrivial conundrum to achieve balanced excited-state energy dissipation to guarantee high NIR-II brightness, photothermal conversion, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. As a powerful tool for balancing radiative and nonradiative decays, aggregation-induced emission luminogens (AIEgens) are emerging as a promising frontier in developing “one-for-all” phototheranostic agents, while their phototheranostic performance needs to be further improved. In this contribution, we designed and synthesized two positional isomers, 5BT-PBPT and 6BT-PBPT, by attaching donors at the 5- and 6-positions of the benzo[b]thiophene (BT) segment, respectively, to investigate the effect of positional isomerism on the phototheranostic performance of NIR-II AIEgens. Interestingly, both experimental and computational results demonstrate that the isomerization affords great strength in tuning energy levels, structural conformations, aggregation behaviors, and excited-state energy dissipation. Consequently, a sweet spot for fully utilizing excitation energy was achieved in 5BT-PBPT nanoparticles (NPs), which exhibited not only strong NIR absorption but also high NIR-II fluorescence brightness, strong ROS production, and excellent photothermal conversion efficiency (η). Benefiting from this, 5BT-PBPT NPs afforded superior performance in the “one-for-all” phototheranostics for orthotopic breast tumor treatment. This study fully demonstrates the effectiveness of the isomeric engineering strategy in comprehensively improving the phototheranostic capabilities of NIR-II AIEgens and thereby provides an effective approach for the construction of high-performance NIR-II “one-for-all” phototheranostic agents.

title:
Low-Temperature
Aqueous Upgrading of Waste PET Plastics
into Metal–Organic Frameworks with Confined PdNi Clusters for
High-Performance Semihydrogenation of Alkynes
content:
Abstract
The selective semihydrogenation of alkynes to alkenes is an important industrial process for the production of bulk and fine chemicals. However, the activity and selectivity trade-off of alkyne hydrogenation has been a long-standing challenge, due to undesirable overhydrogenation or insufficient activity of the designed catalysts. Here, we report a sustainable route for high-performance alkyne hydrogenation using a metal–organic framework (MOF) confined PdNi cluster (PdcNi) catalyst, synthesized directly from waste polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastics under low-temperature aqueous conditions. The PdcNi@UiO-66 catalyst with dispersed Pd clusters anchored on Ni clusters not only maximizes Pd utilization but also establishes a new pathway for the recycling of plastics. Importantly, when employed as a catalyst for phenylacetylene semihydrogenation, PdcNi@UiO-66 exhibited outstanding activity and selectivity, achieving a turnover frequency (TOF) of up to 67,470 h–1 at 65 °C. This performance significantly surpasses that of previously reported catalysts and is nearly 20 times higher than that of the commercial Lindlar catalyst. DFT calculations combined with experimental results reveal that the PdcNi cluster exhibits a moderate adsorption strength toward both reactants and target products, compared with its nanoparticle and single-atom counterparts. This balanced adsorption leads to a more favorable thermodynamic tendency for styrene desorption rather than overhydrogenation, ultimately contributing to the high activity and selectivity. This study demonstrates a direct route to transforming PET waste into high-performance MOF-based catalysts for selective hydrogenation, offering a cost-effective and sustainable solution for plastic recycling and the development of high-performance catalysts.

title:
Mechanistic Insights
of Jahn–Teller Effect
Suppression in High-Entropy Prussian Blue Analogue Cathodes
content:
Abstract
The Jahn–Teller (J-T) effect, as discovered by Hermann Jahn and Edward Teller in 1937, often causes lattice distortion and structural instability in Mn-based battery materials. Recent studies suggest that high-entropy design may help suppress J-T distortion, yet the underlying mechanism remains largely elusive due to their compositional complexity and structural disorder. Herein, using a Mn-based Prussian blue analogue as a case study, we employed a machine learning interatomic potential combined with synchrotron extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy (EXAFS) to elucidate the fundamental mechanism of the J-T suppression in high-entropy materials. Unexpectedly, EXAFS spectra reveal the absence of the typical J-T Mn–N bond-length splitting in our high-entropy Prussian blue analogue sample, but instead a broader Mn–N bond-length distribution. Machine learning-assisted calculations demonstrate the [MnN6] octahedra exhibit randomly oriented distortions along x-, y-, and z-axes in high-entropy lattices, resulting in the local distortion averaging out at the macroscopic scale. Further analysis of the local Mn coordination environment reveals that the high-entropy configuration enhances d-electron delocalization and reduces the energy splitting between Mn dx2–y2 and dz2 orbitals. This allows two structurally and electronically distinct distortion modes to coexist within the lattice, which disrupts long-range cooperative J-T order. Strikingly, the ultralong cycling stability of high-entropy K0.46[Mn0.21Co0.19Ni0.21Cu0.20Zn0.19][Fe(CN)6]0.98·1.69H2O is experimentally demonstrated, achieving 91.0% capacity retention over 50,000 cycles for aqueous ammonium-ion storage, which surpasses all of the Mn-based rechargeable batteries to date. Our study uncovers the microscopic mechanism of J-T suppression in high-entropy materials and provides an effective strategy for designing durable high-entropy battery electrodes.

title:
A DNA Origami Nanodevice
Programs CD20 Spatial Organization
for Selective Apoptosis of Malignant B Cells in Lymphoma Therapy
content:
Abstract
Triggering CD20 clustering to induce B cell apoptosis is considered a promising therapeutic strategy for dysregulated, B cell-driven diseases, yet current methods lack the spatial precision to organize CD20 into defined clusters and fail to discriminate malignant from normal B cells. Here, we describe an intelligent DNA origami nanodevice that integrates an optimized anti-CD20 antibody array with a conformational switch to selectively induce CD20 clustering and apoptosis in B-cell lymphoma. Benefiting from the nanometric precision of DNA origami, we found that arranging anti-CD20 antibodies into a pentavalent array with approximately 10 nm spacing most effectively drives CD20 clustering and downstream apoptosis. Under resting conditions, the nanodevice stays in a closed, tubular shape that conceals the antibody array inside and therefore remains harmless to normal B cells. Upon encountering c-Met expressed on lymphoma B cells, the device unrolls into a planar sheet and exposes the antibody array, triggering potent apoptotic signaling specifically in these malignant cells. In a Raji xenograft mouse model, intravenously injected nanodevices specifically unrolled at the tumor site, inhibited tumor growth by more than 70%, and produced no significant systemic toxicity. By coupling programmable ligand nanopatterning with a shape-changing switch, this DNA origami platform offers a generalizable strategy for receptor-mediated disease therapy.

title:
Photoinduced Ge(II)-Catalyzed
Divergent Functionalization
of Pyridyl Halides via Electron Donor–Acceptor Complexes
content:
Abstract
We report a photoinduced Ge(II)-catalyzed strategy for divergent functionalization of pyridyl halides that leverages in situ electron donor–acceptor (EDA) complex formation to catalytically generate pyridyl radicals, enabling aryl, alkynyl, and alkenyl couplings under mild, protic conditions without an external photocatalyst. Notably, the protocol exhibits excellent chemoselectivity for pyridyl C–X bonds, leaving other aryl halides, including those bearing electron-withdrawing substituents, intact. The protocol further enables unique transformations, including complete C8-selective coupling with 7-aminoquinoline and the modular assembly of benzo[f]isoquinolines from alkenyl boron reagents. Mechanistic studies support an EDA-mediated radical pathway. This work provides a sustainable platform for the divergent functionalization of pyridyl halides and expands the application of main-group elements in catalytic EDA chemistry.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Operando Time-Resolved
Spectroelectrochemical Microscopy
Reveals Distinct Electron Depletion Pathways in Electrocatalysis
content:
Abstract
Understanding electrocatalysis requires direct knowledge of how charge carriers are distributed and consumed at active sites under the operating conditions. However, the spatiotemporal dynamics of injected electrons in working catalysts remain largely inaccessible, hindering a mechanistic understanding of catalytic heterogeneity. Here, we develop an operando time-resolved spectroelectrochemical microscopy that enables direct and quantitative mapping of electron density with microsecond temporal resolution and micrometer spatial resolution. Using monolayer MoS2 as a model system, we directly visualize the spatial redistribution and depletion of electrochemically injected electrons during the hydrogen evolution reaction. We observe pronounced site-specific electron depletion that correlates with catalytic activity and further identify two distinct mechanisms governing charge loss: reaction-limited depletion at highly active sites, including edges and Pt-functionalized sites, and injection-limited depletion in bilayer regions. These results establish a quantitative link between local charge carrier dynamics and catalytic activity and provide a general framework for probing nanoscale carrier dynamics in electrocatalysts.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Unraveling Water Balances
behind Salt Formation in
CO 2  Reduction Electrolyzers
content:
Abstract
Salt precipitation in CO2 electrolyzers remains a critical barrier to long-term stability, yet the underlying water-salt transport and balance are poorly understood. Here, we established a quantitative mass balance framework to account for water entering and leaving the cathode chamber from all possible sources and across different phases, thereby elucidating the origin of bicarbonate salt formation. We revealed that although the inlet CO2 stream typically flows through a water bubbler, it is often not fully saturated with water vapor and thus results in significant liquid water evaporation inside the cathode chamber. Although water crossover from the anolyte to the cathode is, in principle, sufficient to dissolve the cotransported K+ as carbonate species (or even bicarbonate in some cases), evaporation reduces the effective local liquid water-to-K+ ratio, leading to salt precipitation. Conversely, excessive humidification suppresses salt formation but induces electrode wetting and flooding, highlighting a fundamental trade-off between dehydration-induced crystallization and overhumidification-driven mass transport limitations. Together, these findings establish water management as a governing principle for stabilizing CO2 electrolyzers and provide engineering guidelines for controlling salt formation in electrochemical reactor systems.

title:
Uncovering Microbial
Nitrogenous Chemical Diversity
through Isotope-Guided Molecular Networking
content:
Abstract
Nitrogen-containing natural products are pivotal sources of bioactive molecules. However, their comprehensive investigation by metabolomics remains challenging due to background interference from primary metabolites and their high structural diversity including peptides, alkaloids, nucleosides, and others. Here, we present NitroVISION, an integrated pipeline that combines stable isotope labeling with targeted molecular networking to selectively detect nitrogen-containing metabolites from a complex mixture. Applied to five well-characterized Streptomyces strains, NitroVISION identified 42 nitrogen-containing natural products across 23 distinct compound classes, from which we characterized menaxinnamide, a new subclass of nonribosomal peptides incorporating a methylnaphthoquinone unit, and octapiperamide, a novel ribosomal peptide featuring a unique piperazine ring. Our work reveals the hidden chemical space of nitrogenous natural products and paves the way for the systematic exploration of microbial metabolic dark matter.

title:
Experimental
Investigation of CO  2  /CH  4   Competitive Adsorption Behaviors
in Shale under Different Feed Gas Injection Methods
content:
Abstract
Understanding the CO2 and CH4 competitive adsorption behavior is crucial for the engineering optimization of the CO2-enhanced shale gas recovery (CO2-ESGR) process. Most studies evaluate CO2 and CH4 competitive adsorption behaviors by simultaneously injecting their mixed gases, which does not reflect real conditions, as CH4 initially exists in the reservoir and CO2 is injected at a later stage. Whether premixed experiments can adequately represent this sequential process therefore remains unclear. In this study, a comparison of different competitive adsorption measurement methods, including premixed CO2 and CH4 (CO2 and CH4 coinjection) and CO2 huff-and-puff (CO2 injection into a CH4-preadsorbed shale sample), was conducted under different temperature and pressure conditions. The results show that that competitive adsorption is strongly dependent on the injection pathway. With increasing pressure, huff-and-puff showed a steeper rise in CO2 uptake and a decline in residual CH4, whereas premixed adsorption showed a slower increase in CO2 uptake and a slight increase in CH4 uptake. Under the same equilibrium conditions, huff-and-puff retained higher adsorption capacity for both gases. In both pathways, shale preferentially adsorbed CO2 over CH4, and the adsorption selectivity coefficient of CO2 over CH4 (SCO2/CH4) decreased with the increase of pressure. Nevertheless, huff-and-puff maintained higher adsorption selectivity over comparable pressure ranges and increased with the initial pressure of CH4. By accounting for the sequential injection history, huff-and-puff adsorption provides a more reliable basis for evaluating CO2 storage potential and CH4 recovery in CO2-ESGR.

title:
CO 2  Enhanced Hydrocarbon Recovery in Organic-Rich
Shales: Insights from 500 MHz  1 H NMR
content:
Abstract
CO2 huff-and-puff has emerged as a promising approach for enhanced oil recovery in unconventional source rock shales, yet the underlying recovery mechanisms remain difficult to isolate and quantify. Here, high-field 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy was used to investigate in situ CO2–shale interactions in a preserved, intact slim source rock plug. CO2 was stepwise loaded from 0 to 6000 psi and unloaded back to 0 psi at 40 °C. At each pressure step, 500 MHz 1H spectra were acquired and deconvoluted into two Lorentzian peaks representing pore fluid and one Gaussian peak representing kerogen. Pressure-dependent changes in the integrals and line widths of these peaks were used to investigate hydrocarbon depletion from the rock sample and CO2-induced changes in molecular mobility of kerogen and pore fluids. In control experiments, helium injections up to 2500 psi produced no measurable changes in the NMR spectra. In contrast, CO2 injections caused pronounced, pressure-dependent changes in intensities and line widths of 1H NMR signals, revealing mixing with pore fluids and penetration into the kerogen matrix. Both pore fluid and kerogen spectra changed markedly as CO2 entered the supercritical regime above 1000 psi at 40 °C, indicating a distinct transition in molecular mobility. Above 4000 psi, substantial light hydrocarbon evaporation from the plug left heavier, less-mobile components in the pores, resulting in broader NMR peaks. Analysis of the complete loading–unloading cycle indicated that approximately 24.5% of the initial pore fluid was produced, dominated by late-stage high-pressure CO2 loading. These results demonstrate that high-field 1H NMR can quantify hydrocarbon recovery while resolving molecular-scale CO2 interactions with different components in source rock shales that are not easily accessible by conventional mass-balance methods.

title:
Evolution of In Situ Wettability and Capillary Displacements
in Carbonate Rocks: The Effect of Injection Brine Composition
content:
Abstract
Ion-specific interactions at fluid-mineral interfaces play a critical role in controlling wettability and multiphase flow in porous materials. In this study, a series of two-phase flow experiments were conducted on miniature oil-wet carbonate cores to investigate how aqueous chemistry regulates dynamic wettability evolution and pore-scale displacement behavior. Companion cores were conditioned using a common aging protocol to establish comparable mean oil-wet states and subsequently subjected to waterflooding under controlled chemical environments. Fluid configurations and in situ geometric contact angles were characterized at successive imaging stages using high-resolution X-ray microcomputed tomography. As wettability evolved in response to controlled aqueous chemistry toward less oil-wet states, the pathways of pore-scale invasion were correspondingly reorganized. Morphology-based analysis of the oil displaced between consecutive imaging stages quantified the relative volume contributions of piston-like invasion and wetting-layer drainage to incremental oil recovery. Piston-like invasion dominated initial displacement, whereas wetting-layer drainage accounted for most later-stage recovery during low-salinity flooding. These stage-dependent contributions connect brine-associated wettability changes with the pore-scale processes responsible for oil mobilization.

title:
Displacement-History Control of Low-Salinity Waterflooding
in Chalk: Insights from Early Brine Switching
content:
Abstract
Low-salinity waterflooding is widely recognized as a promising enhanced oil recovery method, yet its reported performance remains highly variable because the observed response reflects not only brine composition, but also the displacement state of the porous medium at the time the injected brine is introduced. While most previous studies have focused on optimizing brine chemistry, the mechanistic role of injection timing and displacement history has received far less attention. In this study, we investigate how the timing of brine switching governs low-salinity response in chalk by introducing an early tertiary flooding design, in which the injected brine is switched immediately after secondary brine breakthrough. This approach enables controlled probing of an intermediate saturation state representative of the reservoir region just behind the advancing flood front. The resulting recovery behavior was interpreted together with ion chromatography measurements to track brine displacement and chemical-front propagation. The results show that the apparent efficiency of low-salinity flooding is strongly governed by displacement history. Conventional tertiary injection produced negligible incremental recovery, whereas early tertiary injection of diluted seawater yielded 11.3% additional oil recovery (11.8% when formation water was used as the tertiary brine), comparable to values commonly reported for secondary low-salinity flooding. Ion chromatography revealed that the onset of tertiary oil production occurred only after the preceding brine had been displaced from the core. This indicates that chemical-front propagation, in situ mixing, and fluid accessibility govern when the tertiary response becomes observable. The data also confirmed transient formation-water banks ahead of the injected brine front. These findings indicate that tertiary low-salinity performance is controlled not only by brine composition, but also by the fluid occupancy and chemical accessibility inherited from prior flooding at the moment of brine introduction. More broadly, the results support viewing secondary, early tertiary, and conventional tertiary flooding as successive stages of flood maturity, each probing a different displacement state of the reservoir. Conventional tertiary corefloods may therefore underestimate the observable low-salinity response by introducing the modified brine only after extensive prior brine invasion and oil displacement. This highlights injection timing as a key mechanistic variable in chalk waterflooding.

title:
Deep Learning-Based
Recognition and Quantitative Characterization
of CO 2  Hydrate Growth in Microfluidic Porous Media
content:
Abstract
The growth and morphological evolution of CO2 hydrates in marine sediments are recognized as highly significant for hydrate-based CO2 sequestration (HBCS). However, it remains challenging for their pore-scale processes to be directly characterized via macroscopic parameters. To ensure that issues such as weak boundaries, matrix texture interference, and internal pores in microfluidic CO2 hydrate images are addressed, an automated recognition and quantitative analysis method based on deep learning semantic segmentation was developed in this study. An image data set was compiled from microfluidic experiments, and four models (U-Net, Res-U-Net, Attention U-Net, and DeepLabv3+) were subsequently trained and compared. The results demonstrated that the hydrate regions were effectively identified by all four models. Among these, optimal performance was exhibited by the Attention U-Net model, with hydrate intersection over union (IoU) and Dice coefficients being recorded at 0.951 and 0.975, respectively. Furthermore, the optimal model was applied to continuous image sequences; consequently, the dynamic tracking of the CO2 hydrate growth process was achieved, and parameters, including hydrate saturation, internal pore ratio, and growth rate, were extracted. It was revealed that internal pores in the saline system are predominantly distributed within the hydrate envelope and that the inhibitory effect of the saline solution on hydrate growth is strengthened as the ion concentration is increased. At NaCl concentrations of 1, 3, and 5 wt %, the average growth rates were reduced by approximately 10.6%, 33.1%, and 70.4%, respectively. Among the various 3 wt % saline solutions tested, the lowest growth rate was observed in the NaCl system, whereas relatively high areal growth rates were maintained by the KCl, MgCl2, and CaCl2 systems. Thus, a reproducible pixel-level recognition and quantitative characterization approach for the microfluidic CO2 hydrate growth process is provided by our proposed method.

title: Quantifying Sodium Metal SEI Dissolution and Relation to Corrosion Using Quartz Crystal Microbalance
content:
Abstract
Sodium-metal batteries present a more abundant alternative to lithium-based batteries, with high theoretical capacity and comparable reduction potential. Ether electrolytes perform well in sodium-metal batteries under continuous cycling and are presumed to have a stable solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI). However, the solubility of sodium SEI components is a cause for concern, and SEI evolution during calendar aging is not commonly studied for the ether sodium-metal system. In this work, SEI mass formation and dissolution are quantitatively measured for NaPF6 in diglyme. For varying potential hold levels, significant SEI dissolution is observed, from 55 to 76% of the originally formed SEI. Characterization shows that in addition to organic component dissolution, inorganic salts such as NaF and NaxPOyFz are unstable in SEI during open circuit rest. This instability results in continuous corrosion of sodium metal during calendar aging, highlighting an important understanding and concern of SEI stability in sodium-metal batteries.

title: Weak-Solvating Carboxylate Ester Electrolyte Enables Hybrid Interphase via Cooperative Additives toward Wide-Temperature Sodium Metal Batteries
content:
Abstract
Fast Na+ transport and durable interfacial stability remain challenging for wide-temperature Na- metal batteries. To address these issues, we developed a synergistic solvation-interphase regulation strategy by integrating methyl propanoate (MP) with a combined VC/NaDFOB additive pair. MP modifies the Na+ solvation sheath and facilitates Na+ desolvation, while VC and NaDFOB cooperatively generate a mechanically robust hybrid organicinorganic interphase. This coupled regulation enables enhanced ion transport and interfacial stability over a broad temperature range. The EC/EMC/MP + VC/NaDFOB electrolyte exhibits an ionic conductivity of 2.52 mS cm–1 at –40 ̊C and an increased Na+ transference number. Na||Na3V2(PO4)3 cells retain 96.5% of their initial capacity after 1000 cycles with an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.98% at room temperature. At –20 ̊C, the cells deliver 69.4 mAh g–1 for over 900 cycles, corresponding to 82% of their room-temperature capacity. This work establishes a practical solvation-interphase regulation approach for wide-temperature Na- metal batteries.

title: High-Performance LiNiO 2  Cathodes through Microstructural Engineering
content:
Abstract
LiNiO2 (LNO) is a promising high-capacity cathode, but its practical application is hindered by severe structural and microstructural instability. Herein, we develop a two-step calcination strategy that decouples lithiation from Ta introduction. This approach promotes the segregation of a Ta-rich phase at grain boundaries, producing nanosized, radially aligned primary particles that mitigate strain and suppress microcracking. It also preserves a layered–rocksalt nanostructured multiphase that reversibly transforms into a layered–spinel-like state during charging, which may contribute to structural stability and Li-ion transport. The optimized TS-Ta-LNO delivers 252.7 mAh g–1 and retains 88.4% of its capacity after 100 cycles. Furthermore, a TS-Ta-LNO/Li-metal pouch cell maintains stable voltage profiles under an electric vertical take-off and landing dynamic-load protocol, demonstrating its potential for high-energy, high-power batteries.

title: Electrostatic Contributions of the Extended Environment and Local Catalytic Effects in Bipolar Membranes
content:
Abstract
Catalyst layers are widely used to accelerate water dissociation in bipolar membranes (BPMs), yet their role in defining junction electrostatics and reversible reaction kinetics remains unclear. Here, we probe the electrochemical response of catalyst-containing BPM junctions using open-circuit voltage measurements, polarization analysis, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. We show that catalyst nanoparticles influence both the recovery of the membrane potential and the voltage losses associated with water dissociation and formation at the catalyst layer. These changes reflect coupled effects of catalyst surface chemistry, junction electrostatics, and proton-transfer kinetics. Notably, catalysts that recover the membrane potential do not necessarily reduce overvoltage under applied bias, highlighting that membrane-potential recovery alone is insufficient to predict BPM performance. By combining improvements in membrane-potential recovery and reaction kinetics, catalyst–ionomer interface engineering reduces water-formation losses by up to 65% and increases peak power density for energy storage by more than an order of magnitude.

title: Engineering Flexible Pristine and Core–Shell Triazolate Frameworks with Pressure-Induced Breathing for High-Pressure CO 2  Capture
content:
Abstract
This study presents the synthesis of pristine zinc and cobalt triazolate frameworks (ZnTF and CoTF) and their bimetallic core–shell architectures (ZnTF@CoTF, CoTF@ZnTF) for high-pressure CO2 capture. Utilizing 1,2,4-triazole linkers integrates uncoordinated, nitrogen-rich Lewis basic sites into the pores, enhancing CO2 binding without surface modifications. Crystallographic and computational analyses reveal that these materials adopt flexible cubic lattices capable of pressure-induced "breathing". High-pressure evaluations up to 40 bar demonstrate a striking inverse correlation between the baseline surface area and gas uptake. The CoTF@ZnTF architecture exhibited the lowest intrinsic low-temperature porosity (BET maximum of 18 cm3/g) but achieved the highest high-pressure CO2 capacity of 2.4 mmol/g. This indicates that strongly interacting CO2 molecules provide the thermodynamic energy to physically pry open the constrained lattice, effectively excluding N2. Conversely, the ZnTF@CoTF composite maximized thermodynamic separation, reaching a peak CO2/N2 selectivity of 7.8 with a CO2 uptake of 2.15 mmol/g. Ambient-pressure cyclic testing via QCM-D highlighted the stability advantages of this interfacial locking mechanism. While the pristine CoTF lost 13.4% of its capacity over ten humidity cycles, encapsulating the system within a robust ZnTF shell (ZnTF@CoTF) effectively shielded the vulnerable cobalt phase, retaining 98.0% of its hydrolytic capacity. Ultimately, engineering interfacial lattice mismatch in core–shell triazolate heterostructures successfully balances dynamic structural flexibility, localized Lewis basicity, and hydrolytic shielding, yielding highly durable solid physisorbents for scalable carbon mitigation.

title: Design of Liquid Metal/Ionic Liquid Composite Gel Electrodes for Stretchable Li-Ion Battery Applications
content:
Abstract
Stretchable Li-ion batteries are promising power sources for next-generation wearable and deformable electronics; however, designing battery electrodes that simultaneously provide electronic conductivity, ionic conductivity, and mechanical stretchability remains challenging. Here, we develop liquid metal/ionic liquid composite gel electrodes containing Li4Ti5O12 as stretchable mixed electronic–ionic conducting electrodes for Li-ion batteries. Ag powder was introduced as a filler for Ga-In liquid metal, enabling partial alloying at the Ag/LM interface; the resulting improved wettability enhanced the continuity of the metallic conductive network. Consequently, the electronic conductivity reached the order of 103 S cm–1, substantially higher than that of Ni-based counterparts. Tensile and electromechanical measurements showed that the liquid metal (LM) phase maintained stretchability (>50% strain) and suppressed resistance increases during deformation by bridging gaps between metallic particles. Selection of the ionic liquid (IL) component further improved ionic conductivity and charge–discharge performance. Using a thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU)-based composite gel electrode, reversible charge–discharge operation was demonstrated even under 50% strain. However, post-cycling analysis revealed electrochemically induced degradation of TPU, accompanied by deterioration in mechanical integrity. These results demonstrate IL/LM composite gel electrodes as a promising materials platform for stretchable Li-ion battery electrodes while identifying polymer electrochemical stability as a key requirement for durable deformable energy-storage devices.

title: Effect of Depletion Region Width on Self-Powered UV–Visible Photoresponse of Cu 2 O-In 2 O 3  Planar p–n Junction Photodetectors
content:
Abstract
Self-powered photodetectors have garnered significant attention due to their potential applications in optical communication, remote sensing, and imaging. This work presents p-Cu2O/n-In2O3 type-II heterojunction photodetectors via sputtering, achieving self-powered photodetection across the ultraviolet-visible spectrum. Here, Cu2O-In2O3 planar p–n junction thin films are developed with different depletion region widths (DRWs) of 1.5, 3.0, and 4.5 mm. Optical studies confirm that the In2O3 film exhibits strong ultraviolet (UV) absorbance and a wide bandgap of 3.35 eV. In contrast, the Cu2O film exhibits strong UV–visible absorbance with a narrow bandgap of 2.25 eV. Among the devices, the device with a DRW of 3.0 mm achieves higher photodetector performance, attributed to a stronger electric field and reduced charge-carrier recombination in the depletion region. Consequently, the device with a 3.0 mm DRW shows the highest responsivity (Rλ) of 4.8 mA/W, 9.4 mA/W, 13.8 mA/W, and 4.4 mA/W and detectivity (D*) of 2.14 × 1010 Jones, 4.19 × 1010 Jones, 6.15 × 1010 Jones, and 1.98 × 1010 Jones at 380, 460, 530, and 630 nm illuminations, respectively, even at lower incident optical power densities. Although the fabricated Cu2O-In2O3 p–n junction self-powered photodetector devices exhibit relatively modest figures of merit, they offer distinct advantages: self-powered operation, a broad spectral response in the UV–visible region, and stable photoresponse, highlighting their potential for low-power optoelectronic applications.

title: High-Entropy-Inspired Trace Multi-cation Doping Enables Structural Reinforcement and Accelerated Na-Ion Transport in Mn-Based Layered Cathodes
content:
Abstract
Owing to their open Na+ diffusion pathways and high theoretical specific capacity, P2-type layered oxides are regarded as promising cathode materials for sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). In this study, we propose a high-entropy trace doping strategy and employ a high-temperature solid-state method to incorporate five metal elements (Mg, Al, Co, Zn, and Ti) into P2-Na0.67MnO2, successfully synthesizing the P2-Na0.67Mg0.02Al0.02Co0.02Zn0.02Ti0.02Mn0.9O2 (HE-NMO) cathode material. Structural characterizations reveal that high-entropy trace doping effectively regulates anisotropic grain growth, while the relatively homogeneous distribution of multi-element ions within the particles modifies the local ordering environment and regulates the TM–O bonding framework. Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that HE-NMO exhibits enhanced Na+ diffusion kinetics and a higher pseudocapacitance contribution compared with undoped NMO. Benefiting from the complementary effects of structural stabilization and accelerated ion transport, HE-NMO delivers a high discharge capacity of 169.6 mAh g–1 at 50 mA g–1 and maintains 80.1 mAh g–1 at 2 A g–1, together with 78.7% capacity retention after 300 cycles at 500 mA g–1. This work provides a high-entropy-inspired trace multi-cation doping strategy for designing structurally robust and kinetically favorable P2-type layered oxide cathodes toward advanced sodium-ion storage.

title: Triazole-Decorated Porphyrin Cathodes Enabling Reversible Chloroaluminate Storage for High-PerformanceAluminum-Ion Batteries
content:
Abstract
The emergence of rechargeable aluminum-ion batteries (AIBs) as potential successors in the field of energy storage is predicated on the substantial theoretical capacity, natural availability, cost-effectiveness, and intrinsic stability of metallic aluminum. Nevertheless, the intense electrostatic forces between multivalent aluminum ions and their host structures frequently result in retarded reaction rates and compromised cycling durability, presenting impediments to the engineering of superior AIBs cathodes. Herein, we report 5,10,15,20-tetrakis[4-(1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)phenyl]porphyrin (H2TTPP), a triazole-functionalized porphyrin, as an efficient organic cathode for AIBs. The constructed H2TTPP-based AIBs exhibit a substantial operational potential of 1.495 V and a primary charging capacity of 202.2 mAh g–1 at a current density of 40 mA g–1, while demonstrating superior rate performance up to 1000 mA g–1 and exceptional cyclability surpassing 10,000 cycles at 500 mA g–1. Further, at 80 mA g–1, the H2TTPP cathode's thermal performance was assessed between 40 and 70 °C, with the high capacity increasing to 216.3 mAh g–1 at 70 °C, while maintaining over 80% Coulombic efficiency (CE). Combined UV–vis spectroscopy, N K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and ex situ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy demonstrate that reversible interactions between N active sites and chloroaluminate ions govern the charge-storage process. In addition, cable-type AIBs maintain stable electrochemical performance under mechanical bending.

title: Interface-Engineered Polypyrrole/WS 2  Heterostructures for High-Voltage Symmetric Supercapacitors
content:
Abstract
Aqueous electrolytes in supercapacitors are constrained by a narrow operating voltage window, limiting energy density and practical applicability thereof. To overcome this, organic electrolytes offer a promising approach to achieve higher operating voltages while maintaining excellent energy and power densities. The current study focuses on the employability of LiClO4 in a propylene carbonate:ethylene carbonate:ethyl acetate electrolyte with interface-engineered tungsten disulfide (WS2) nanoparticles (NPs) embedded in polypyrrole (PPy) via a facile in-situ route with varying WS2 NP loadings (5 and 10 wt %) to elucidate their influence on the electrochemical performance and widen the potential window in a symmetric liquid-configured prototype device. The structure and morphology of the heterostructures were systematically examined through various analytical tools. The PPy/WS2 heterostructure electrode containing WS2 NPs with a loading of 5 wt % exhibits the optimal performance, delivering a specific capacitance of 231.7 F g–1 at a sweep rate of 5 mV s–1. The symmetric device achieved a high operating voltage of 2.4 V, corresponding to 32 Wh kg–1 energy density and 1221.7 W kg–1 power density at 1 A g–1, along with 79% sustainability for 10,000 charge–discharge cycles. Furthermore, the successful operation of an LED panel and a small DC fan highlights the practical applicability of the assembled prototype.

title: Toward High-Entropy Halide and Chalcohalide Semiconductors for Photocatalysis
content:
Abstract
High-entropy design has expanded from metallic alloys to compositionally complex oxides, chalcogenides, and, more recently, halide semiconductors. By distributing several elements over one or more crystallographic sublattices, this strategy can generate properties that are inaccessible through conventional dilute doping, including nonlinear bandgap tuning, modified defect chemistry, lattice distortion, and enhanced chemical stability. Moreover, configurational entropy should be thought not only in terms of compositional variation (alloying) but also in terms of different microstructural polymorphisms and engineered disorder. Metal halide perovskites and perovskite-inspired materials offer unusually broad compositional and structural spaces, yet high-entropy design has only started to be investigated in these systems. Metal chalcohalides provide an equally promising and largely unexplored platform, combining the electronic diversity of halides with the stronger bonding and frequently superior water stability of chalcogenides. In this Perspective, we first discuss how the term high-entropy should be applied in the realm of multinary semiconductors. Then, we identify promising compositional spaces for high-entropy halides and chalcohalides and evaluate synthetic strategies to achieve them experimentally, including automated combinatorial routes and non-standard mechanochemical synthesis. Eventually, we examine the potential of these emerging materials in photocatalytic applications. The Perspective ends by discussing current bottlenecks and potential routes for the development of this emerging field.

title: Interfacial Engineering of Zn–Ag Bimetallic Catalysts to Enable Efficient CO 2 -to-CO Conversion in Both Acidic and Alkaline Media
content:
Abstract
Electrochemical CO2 reduction (CO2RR) offers a promising strategy for converting greenhouse gases into value-added chemicals; however, maintaining high selectivity across diverse pH environments remains challenging. Acidic electrolytes enhance carbon efficiency by suppressing carbonate formation but simultaneously favor the hydrogen evolution reaction, whereas alkaline media provide high activity while causing CO2 loss through carbonate/bicarbonate formation. Here, we report a nanoporous-Zn–Ag catalyst with engineered interfacial sites that enables efficient CO2-to-CO conversion in both acidic and alkaline environments. The catalyst was synthesized by CTAB-assisted electrodeposition followed by controlled galvanic replacement, generating Zn–Ag interfaces that optimize CO2RR activity. In a flow-cell configuration, the optimized Zn–Ag catalyst prepared with 0.02 mM AgNO3 (denoted ZnAg-1) achieved a Faradaic efficiency (FE) exceeding 90% for CO2 conversion into CO and formic acid production at –100 mA cm–2 in both 1.0 M KOH (pH 14) and 0.05 M H2SO4 + 1.0 M KCl (pH 1), with stable operation long-term electrolysis. Interestingly, the product distribution depended strongly on electrolyte pH:CO selectivity reached 87% in alkaline media but decreased to ∼71% under acidic conditions, while formate/formic acid contribution increased from 3 to 20%. Density functional theory free-energy calculations using representative Zn–Ag interfacial models suggest that local Zn–Ag coordination can lower the thermodynamic requirement for *COOH formation and facilitate CO desorption; the potential-limiting PCET step is *COOH formation from *CO2 (ΔG = 0.34 eV), corresponding to UL = –0.34 V vs RHE. The experimentally observed increase in formate/formic acid under acidic conditions is tentatively attributed to the competing *OCHO pathway, which is not explicitly evaluated in the present DFT calculations. These results demonstrate that interfacial engineering in bimetallic catalysts enables efficient CO2RR across a wide pH range, providing a viable pathway toward industrial implementation.

title: Metal–Organic Framework Assisted Sample Preparation Enables High‐Depth Proteomics of Laser‐Captured Trace Kidney Microregions
content:
A metal–organic framework‐assisted sample preparation workflow enables high‐depth proteomic profiling of laser‐captured kidney microregions as small as 0.25 mm2. Greater proteome coverage and quantitative reproducibility are obtained than with conventional filter‐aided sample preparation, while region‐resolved analysis reveals distinct cortical and medullary proteomes and coordinated inflammatory and mitochondrial protein changes in sepsis‐associated acute kidney injury.








ABSTRACT
Region‐resolved proteomics based on laser capture microdissection (LCM) enables molecular characterization of solid organ heterogeneity but is limited by severe protein loss and shallow coverage in trace tissue samples. Here, we adapted and optimized a quadruple boronic acid‐rich lanthanide metal–organic framework (qMOFs)‐aided sample preparation workflow (MASP) for LCM‐derived trace kidney tissues and benchmarked its performance against conventional filter‐aided sample preparation (FASP) across tissue inputs of 0.25–1.5 mm2. Notably, MASP identified at least 6248 protein groups from 0.25 mm2 of tissue, approximately three times the maximum number of 2042 protein groups identified by FASP from 1.5 mm2 of tissue. We further applied this workflow to region‐resolved proteomic profiling of renal cortex and medulla in a cecal ligation and puncture (CLP)‐induced sepsis‐associated acute kidney injury (SA‐AKI) mouse model, identifying regional proteomic differences between cortical and medullary microregions and changes in mitochondrial protein abundance in cortical samples from Sham and CLP mice. This work extends MASP to microdissected solid tissues and provides a robust platform for high‐depth region‐resolved proteomics of heterogeneous organs, enabling systematic investigation of region‐specific molecular alterations in disease.

title: Interfacial Copper Oxidation Under an Applied Alternating Electric Field and a Water‐Soluble Caramel Support Enable Clean, Low‐Defect Transfer of Large‐Area Graphene
content:
Interfacial copper oxidation under an applied alternating electric field weakens the graphene–Cu interaction, while a water‐soluble caramel support enables conformal contact, mechanical delamination, and clean aqueous removal. Together, these two processes reduce transfer‐induced damage and support‐derived contamination during large‐area graphene transfer, resulting in smoother graphene films, lower relative p‐type doping, and improved carrier transport compared with conventional PMMA‐assisted transfer. This strategy provides a practical and scalable route toward high‐fidelity graphene device fabrication and integration.








ABSTRACT
Graphene is a promising platform for next‐generation electronics, yet conventional transfer from catalytic metals often introduces cracks, wrinkles, polymer residues, and unintended doping that compromise device performance. Here, we report a synergistic transfer strategy combining interfacial Cu oxidation under an applied 50 Hz AC electric field with a water‐soluble caramel support. Under otherwise identical aqueous‐treatment conditions, the AC‐field‐treated graphene/Cu exhibits faster oxidation propagation and lower spatial heterogeneity than the water‐only control, producing a Cu2O‐rich interfacial state favorable for subsequent graphene delamination. The caramel support, prepared from sucrose and corn syrup, provides tunable thermomechanical compliance, conformal contact with diverse target substrates, weak interaction with graphene, and facile aqueous removal. Using this approach, graphene was successfully transferred at the 4‐inch scale onto SiO2/Si and other substrates, with a root‐mean‐square surface roughness of 0.73 nm. Compared with PMMA‐transferred controls, the resulting graphene exhibited reduced support‐derived contamination, fewer transfer‐induced structural perturbations, weaker p‐type doping, and improved carrier transport. This work provides a scalable route for clean, low‐damage, large‐area graphene transfer and device integration.

title: Stabilizing Interfaces in Magnesium Solid‐State Batteries via High‐Throughput Coating Design
content:
High‐throughput calculations reveal the intrinsically narrow electrochemical stability window of magnesium solid electrolytes and their chemical incompatibility with cathodes. To address this limitation, we systematically screen 19 098 Mg‐containing compounds and identify seven promising coating materials that effectively mitigate interfacial reactions, providing practical design guidelines for stable solid‐state magnesium battery interfaces.








ABSTRACT
To meet the growing demand for affordable and safe electrochemical energy storage systems with high energy density, all‐solid‐state magnesium‐ion batteries (ASSMBs) have emerged as promising candidates, because magnesium is naturally abundant and offers high volumetric capacity. However, the electrochemical stability of magnesium solid electrolytes (SEs), as well as their chemical compatibility with magnesium cathodes, remains underexplored. Herein, we assess the electrochemical stability window (ESW) of magnesium SEs and evaluate their interfacial reactivity with magnesium cathodes by calculating the decomposition energy for SE–cathode pairs. Consequently, the mismatch between the ESW of magnesium SEs and cathode requirements should be addressed, underscoring the need for protective strategies. Accordingly, a high‐throughput screening for relevant coating materials is conducted, identifying 14 experimentally observed candidates from 19 098 magnesium‐containing inorganic compounds after thermodynamical screening. These compounds are further evaluated by computing their migration barriers for vacancy hopping, excluding seven compounds with exceptionally high vacancy‐diffusion barriers and leaving seven remaining coating candidates. Following this hierarchical screening, seven Mg‐containing compounds remained as particularly appealing candidates: MgBr2, Mg3B7ClO13, MgBHO3, Mg3Si(O2F)2, MgH8(ClO2)2, Mg3Si4(HO6)2, and Mg7P2(HO2)8. This work provides fundamental insights into magnesium SEs and their interfacial stability, establishing a rational design framework to enhance overall cell performance in ASSMBs.

title: Resolving Real‐Time Interfacial Dynamics on Garnet‐Based Solid‐State Electrolytes via Snapshot Operando XPS
content:
This work establishes snapshot operando x‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) as a compelling laboratory‐based technique for real‐time probing of dynamic interfaces in solid‐state batteries. By combining second‐scale temporal resolution with complementary HAXPES depth profiling, the methodology enables direct observation of electrochemical processes that are inaccessible using conventional XPS measurements.








ABSTRACT
Unveiling interfacial dynamics in solid‐state batteries under operando conditions remains a major challenge in solid‐state battery research, largely due to the limited temporal resolution of conventional analytical techniques. Here, we introduce a laboratory‐based operando x‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) methodology employing a snapshot spectral acquisition mode that enables real‐time tracking of interfacial chemistry in solid‐state battery systems. The approach is demonstrated by monitoring electrochemical lithiation occurring in Sb and Cu films deposited on the surface of the Li6.25Al0.25La3Zr2O12 solid‐state electrolyte (SSE). Understanding these processes is critical for developing effective SSE/Li interfacial layers that improve the cycling stability of lithium metal anodes and for advancing anode‐free solid‐state battery architectures. When combined with the static in‐situ non‐destructive depth‐profiling capabilities of hard x‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES), this methodology has strong potential to become a key analytical approach for probing buried interfaces in solid‐state batteries under operando conditions.

title: Mineral Particle Suspensions in Carbonate Electrolyte Enable LiF‐Rich Interphases for Durable Lithium Metal Batteries
content:
Suspending LiF and Li2O particles in carbonate electrolyte promotes defluorination of FEC and LiPF6 via preferential adsorption and electronic polarization, facilitating the formation of LiF‐rich interphases. These robust interphases on both anode and cathode suppress dendrites and parasitic reactions, enabling 2400 h symmetric‐cell cycling and 85.6% capacity retention after 400 full‐cell cycles.








ABSTRACT
The solid electrolyte interphase in lithium metal batteries determines cycling stability but often suffers from the incomplete decomposition of fluorinated components. Herein, we demonstrate that suspending LiF and Li2O particles in a carbonate‐based electrolyte promotes the defluorination of fluoroethylene carbonate and lithium hexafluorophosphate. These particles preferentially adsorb fluorinated electrolyte species and induce electronic polarization, thereby modulating their redox reactivity and facilitating interfacial decomposition toward LiF. The generated LiF, together with the trace dissolution and interfacial reprecipitation of suspended LiF particles, continuously enriches the electrode surface with LiF‐rich inorganic species. This process results in the formation of a bilayer interphase on both the lithium metal anode and LiNi0.6Co0.2Mn0.2O2 cathode, featuring a flexible inner layer and a dense LiF‐rich outer layer. The resulting interphase suppresses lithium dendrites, mitigates parasitic reactions, and enables 2400 h of stable cycling in symmetric cells and 85.6% capacity retention after 400 cycles in full cells. By introducing suspended LiF/Li2O particles to regulate the interfacial decomposition of fluorinated electrolyte species, this work provides an effective electrolyte‐design strategy for constructing robust interphases in lithium metal batteries.

title:
Highly Selective Artificial
Lithium Channels
content:
Abstract
Sustainable mining and recycling of lithium (Li) have the potential to offer a secure and reliable global supply of lithium to meet rapidly growing energy-storage demands. Bioinspired technologies have the potential to increase sustainability and reduce the environmental impacts of lithium purification. In this study, we report the design of a class of bioinspired supramolecular membrane channels that, to the best of our knowledge, achieve one of the highest overall Li+ selectivities reported to date for artificial transmembrane ion channels, with conservative lower-limit selectivity estimates of Li+/Na+ ≥ 94, Li+/K+ ≥ 136, Li+/Mg2+ ≥ 286, and Li+/Ca2+ ≥ 228 under electrochemically driven transport conditions, thereby establishing a new benchmark for Li+-selective membrane channels. The single-channel conductance of this channel for Li+ ions was determined to be 13.35 pS, equating to Li+ ion transport rates of approximately 1.34 × 107 ions/s per channel at −160 mV. These channels were constructed using a central-ring pillar[5]arene appended with alkyl chains ending in diphenylphosphine oxide (DPP) ligands. Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that Li+ selectivity arises from coupled hydration-shell retention, ion-ligand coordination at the DPP-functionalized entrance, and confinement effects within the LAP5n10-DPP channel. At the DPP-functionalized entrance, Li+ retains much of its compact hydration shell while engaging the phosphoryl oxygen through a favorable ligand-exchange interaction, whereas Na+ interacts with the DPP region primarily through a water-separated outer-shell geometry, and K+ interacts more strongly with the adjacent hydrophobic/phenyl-rich region. At the central constriction, all ions experience hydration-shell disruption, but divalent Ca2+ and Mg2+ face the largest dehydration penalties because pore passage would require near-complete dehydration of their strongly bound hydration shells.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Smallest
Endohedral Water Cage Featuring a Nonclassic
Polyhedron: Experimental Observation of (H 2 O) 17
content:
Abstract
The structural transition from clustered water molecules to the hydrogen-bonding networks of bulk liquid defines one of the most fundamental problems in physical chemistry, yet the precise size at which the endohedral cages emerge remains experimentally elusive. While theory has long predicted that a fully encapsulated water molecule requires a minimum of 16–23 surrounding molecules, direct experimental identification has been hindered by the difficulty of size selection of neutral clusters. Using infrared spectroscopy coupled to vacuum-ultraviolet threshold photoionization, we provide the first experimental evidence that (H2O)17 forms the smallest water endohedral cage, achieving a decades-standing goal of establishing the molecular limit of a solvation shell. Surprisingly, the oxygen framework of this (H2O)17 cage defines an unprecedented, nonclassic polyhedron with four tetragonal, four pentagonal, and two hexagonal faces that breaks the symmetry constraints of all classical Platonic, Archimedean, and Johnson solids. This work establishes a critical structural precursor to the hydrogen-bonding network topology observed in condensed-phase water and offers new perspectives at the multidisciplinary sciences of mathematics, materials, physics, and chemistry.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Vacancy-Induced
Ligand-Hole Character Redirects Oxygen
Redox in Li-Rich Layered Oxides
content:
Abstract
Li-rich layered oxides access high capacities through the combined participation of transition-metal and oxygen redox, but oxygen oxidation is often coupled with irreversible structural rearrangement and voltage decay. Here, we show that oxygen-vacancy-preconditioning modifies the local Ni–O electronic structure and promotes oxygen-derived ligand-hole character in a Li-rich layered oxide. High-temperature quasi-single-crystal (QSC) formation generates oxygen-deficient local environments while preserving the overall layered framework. Synchrotron spectroscopy combined with density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveals enhanced Ni–O hybridization and redistribution of charge compensation toward oxygen-derived states. Mapping resonant inelastic X-ray scattering further shows earlier oxygen participation during charging, followed by increased delocalization of oxygen-derived holes within hybridized transition-metal–oxygen states. This modified redox pathway suppresses Mn reduction and is coupled to a distinct structural response in which transient lattice environments formed during the initial cycle progressively relax during prolonged cycling, while the layered framework is largely retained. The resulting cathode exhibits reduced voltage hysteresis and voltage decay, together with improved electrochemical reversibility. These results establish a direct connection between vacancy-modified ligand-hole character and oxygen-redox-driven structural relaxation, demonstrating how local electronic structure governs the structural pathway of oxygen-redox-active layered oxides.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Highly Enantioselective
Synthesis of 1,2,3-Trisubstituted
Cyclopropanes through DNA-Catalyzed Johnson–Corey–Chaykovsky
Cyclopropanation
content:
Abstract
Developing enzymatic strategies for diverse reaction manifolds is a major objective in modern biocatalysis. Here, we report the first biocatalytic asymmetric Johnson–Corey–Chaykovsky (JCC) cyclopropanation via DNA catalysis. Unlike conventional small-molecule catalysis, which largely favors trans-cyclopropane formation, DNA catalysis enables diastereoselective access to both cis- and trans-cyclopropanes with excellent enantiocontrol from a single catalytic system. The platform accommodates sulfur ylides as well as amide- and ester-derived sulfoxonium ylides. In particular, phenolic ester-derived sulfoxonium ylides exhibit exceptional cis-selectivity while maintaining excellent stereocontrol, overcoming a longstanding limitation of small-molecule-catalyzed asymmetric JCC reactions. Preliminary mechanistic studies are consistent with a DNA scaffold-mediated pathway that promotes cis-diastereomer formation. Together with its scalability under low catalyst loading, this work establishes a previously inaccessible biocatalytic variant of the JCC reaction and expands the scope of DNA catalysis for diastereoselective synthesis.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Understanding the Instability
Origin for Design of
Robust Pure RuO 2  Anode Catalyst in PEM Water Electrolysis
content:
Abstract
Ruthenium dioxide (RuO2) shows great promise as an acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalyst in proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE), yet its insufficient stability─often attributed to Ru overoxidation─actually has a hidden cause. Herein, we show that the true culprit is instead residual chloride impurities inherited from the most commonly used RuCl3 precursor. Owing to strong Ru–Cl coordination, substantial chlorine residues are trapped in the RuO2 lattice during conventional synthesis; during electrolysis, they gradually leach out, dramatically accelerating Ru dissolution and lattice oxygen loss and triggering structural collapse. Guided by this insight, we developed a small-molecule-assisted synthesis that yields Cl-free RuO2. The resulting catalyst preserves exceptional structural integrity, sustains its initial activity through 80,000 accelerated degradation cycles, and delivers stable PEMWE operation at 500 mA cm–2 for 500 h, outperforming all reported single RuO2 catalysts and rivaling even the best doped or composite Ru-based catalysts. Our findings resolve a long-standing paradox in RuO2 catalysis and establish chloride elimination as a critical design principle for durable oxide electrocatalysts.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Noncovalent Metal–Water
Polarization Governs
Helmholtz Capacitance
content:
Abstract
Electrified metal–water interfaces govern charge storage and electrochemical reactivity, yet the microscopic origin of their metal-dependent Helmholtz capacitance has remained unresolved. Here, we use extensive density functional theory-based ab initio molecular dynamics simulations to reproduce and explain the long-established experimental capacitance trend at fcc(111) metal–water interfaces. We show that this trend is governed primarily by the electrode-side electronic response of the explicit metal–water interface, which controls the effective electron spillover length and, hence, the bias capacitance. This relation remains predictive for cross-geometry Pt/Au systems. Our findings clarify the microscopic origin of metal-dependent Helmholtz capacitance and suggest a physically grounded design principle for electrode materials in sustainable-energy technologies.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title: Revealing the Drying Mechanism in Roll-to-Roll Electrode Manufacturing
content:
Publication date: Available online 25 October 2026

Source: Energy Storage Materials

Author(s): Xinxin Yao, Yaohong Xiao, Xifei Cao, Xiangwei Guo, Jinrong Su, Hanghang Yan, Lei Chen

title:
Gate-to-Gate Life Cycle Assessment of Solidified Natural
Gas Production via Clathrate Hydrate Formation: Environmental Trade-Offs
of Thermodynamic Promoter Selection
content:
Abstract
Solidified natural gas (SNG) is a potential alternative to liquefied and compressed natural gas for natural gas storage, but its environmental performance has not been quantified. This study presents the first life cycle assessment of SNG production via clathrate hydrate formation, comparing unpromoted methane hydrate (sI), methane–tetrahydrofuran (THF) hydrate (sII), and methane–1,3-dioxolane hydrate (sII). A gate-to-gate assessment was performed using ReCiPe 2016 (H) with a functional unit of 1 MJ of natural gas stored as methane hydrate. Since unconverted methane is recycled, all configurations consume the same net quantity of methane, and the higher conversion of the promoted systems (42.0% versus 10.0%) instead reduces electricity demand from 0.116 to approximately 0.030 kW h MJ–1. The unpromoted process had the lowest impact in all 18 midpoint categories, including the lowest global warming potential (0.070 kg CO2-eq MJ–1) and end point single score (1.83 mPt). The global warming potentials of the 1,3-dioxolane- and THF-promoted processes were 3.0 and 4.7 times higher, with promoter production contributing 83% and 89%, respectively. Paired Monte Carlo analysis confirmed these rankings, with 1,3-dioxolane outperforming THF in 87–100% of iterations depending on the category. The ranking was unchanged under a 20-year characterization horizon and would be reversed only if more than 2.5% of the unconverted methane recycle stream were lost, or if the production burden of 1,3-dioxolane were 81% lower than that of its 1,4-dioxane proxy. Thermodynamic promotion therefore increases rather than redistributes environmental burdens, and the stoichiometric promoter makeup, not hydrate formation, is the principal environmental barrier to promoted SNG.

title: Think Simple, Communicate Better
Robust Full-Spectrum-Responsive Multi-junction Tandem Solar Cells via Enhanced Near-Infrared Photon Harvesting
content:
Abstract
Developing robust multi-junction tandem photovoltaics remains constrained by the instability of mixed-halide perovskite subcells, given their dominating contribution to overall power output. Integrating near-infrared (NIR) PbS quantum dots (QDs) with FAPbBr3 and crystalline silicon (c-Si) broadens spectrum utilization while improving overall operational stability by reducing the perovskite power contribution. However, enlarged (100) facets and the trade-off between film thickness and quality limit efficient NIR photon harvesting. Herein, a Lewis-basic dihydrazide molecule achieves universal passivation across diverse PbS QD facets via synergistic lead chelation and hydrogen-bonding interactions. Consequently, 0.8 eV PbS QD solar cells with a 685 nm-thick active layer achieve a short-circuit current density of 41.31 mA cm–2 and a 1100-nm-filtered efficiency of 1.80%. The resulting FAPbBr3/c-Si/PbS triple-junction tandems achieve a promising efficiency of 31.04%, with the perovskite subcell contributing 30.4% of the total power output, demonstrating a well-matched operational lifetime. This work offers a strategic framework for efficient multi-junction tandem photovoltaics.

title: Hot Carrier Cooling Dynamics in Tin Tri-Iodide Perovskites Thin Films
content:
Abstract
Hot carriers (HC) offer a potential route to surpass conventional efficiency limits in solar cells. Generated after light absorption, these high-energy carriers can significantly boost device performance if extracted before dissipating energy as heat. Although HC cooling has been studied in tin-based perovskites, interpreting these dynamics is challenging because high-energy, high-fluence pump pulses required to generate HCs have shallow penetration depths, confining excitation near the surface. In tin-based perovskites, surface properties differ from the bulk, and surface defects may strongly contribute to the optical response. Here, by using pump-push-probe ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy, we photo-excite the semiconductor thin film with a low-energy pump, in a photon density range typical for solar cell operation, making relevant the bulk electronic properties, and selectively re-excite the photo-carriers only once they cool down, enabling direct tracking of HC relaxation in the relevant spectral region while minimizing surface contributions. We track the cooling process in FA0.85Cs0.15SnI3 (FA = Formamidinium) as a benchmark sample and extend the analysis to single-cation FA+, MA+ (MA = methylammonium), and Cs+ tin perovskites. Across all compositions, and at different doping densities, we find cooling timescales in the 150–600 fs time range. These results highlight the central role of phonon-mediated interactions and show that ultrafast cooling fundamentally limits hot carrier extraction in tin halide perovskites.

title: NaPF 6 -Based Battery Electrolytes near a Sodium Metal Electrode: Role of Organic Solvents on Solid Electrolyte Interphase Formation
content:
Abstract
The choice of electrolytes for improved sodium-metal batteries (SMBs) presents a major challenge owing to the complexity of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) between the electrode and electrolyte. Herein, we systematically examine and compare the dissociation mechanism of electrolytes consisting of sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF6) in three different organic solvents with varying polarity (tetrahydrofuran (THF), propylene carbonate (PC), and a mixture of ethylene carbonate and diethyl carbonate (EC:DEC)) on the sodium metal surface using density functional theory (DFT) and ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. For the NaPF6-THF and NaPF6-PC electrolyte systems, the study reveals the strong reducing nature of the PF6– anion, which readily dissociates and dominates over the solvent molecules present in the system. Our analysis reveals that the solvent molecules, THF and PC, are relatively stable against reductive dissociation over sodium metal in their respective electrolyte solutions. Conversely, in the EC:DEC-based electrolyte, SEI formation is derived from both the anion and EC, and DEC molecules remain undissociated within the simulation timescale. Further, the induced charge (electron) density difference approach captures the charge depletion and accumulation on the sodium electrode and electrolyte species, respectively. The analysis of atomic charges and bond order over time reveals the irreversible dissociation of electrolyte species and provides insights into the nature of chemical bonding in Na–F and Na–P species formed in the SEI layer. Furthermore, the results show that THF and EC:DEC-based electrolytes yield SEIs with well-distributed, inorganic-rich species primarily composed of noncovalently bonded Na–F and Na–P species.

title: Ether-Based Ionic Gel Electrolytes with High Ionic Conductivity and High Thermal Stability for Energy Storage Device Applications
content:
Abstract
The current ionic gel electrolyte (IGE) materials cannot simultaneously achieve high ionic conductivity and high thermal stability. The regulatory mechanism of the ether functional groups on the interaction between ions still needs further investigation. Based on the above research status, this work relied on the σ-profile curve of the conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS) to compare the interface characteristics of different ionic liquids (IL). N-methyl-N-methoxyethyl pyrrolidine bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide salt ([C1OC2Pyr][TFSI]) was screened as the ionic conductive source. Poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP) was chosen as the polymer substrate. A series of IGEs were successfully prepared by adjusting the mass ratio of the IL to the substrate material. IGE-3 sample (with an IL to PVDF-HFP mass ratio of 1:3) exhibited excellent comprehensive performance. This ionic gel presented a continuous, uniform, and loose network structure without obvious agglomeration. The thermal stability temperature was up to 380 oC, the electrochemical stability window reached 5.3 V, and the ionic conductivity was 4.25 × 10–3 S·cm–1. IGE-3 was assembled into a supercapacitor (cell-3). The coulombic efficiency of the device reached 97.9% at 1 A·g–1. Based on density functional theory (DFT) calculations, the intermolecular interactions of IL systems with or without ether functional group modifications were obtained using TURBOMOLE software. Therefore, the IGE prepared in this work combines the excellent electrochemical properties of IL with high thermal stability, making it a core electrolyte material with great application potential.

title: Rapid Supercritical Fluid-Based Hydrothermal Synthesis of Na 3 (VOPO 4 ) 2 F as a Cathode Material for Na-Ion Batteries
content:
Abstract
Sodium vanadium oxyfluorophosphates are highly promising cathode materials for large-scale sodium-ion batteries due to their robust NASICON-type structure, high theoretical capacity (up to ≈130 mAh g–1), and elevated operating potential (≈3.8 V). Yet, the widespread commercial adoption is stalled by the materials’ poor intrinsic electronic conductivity and the complex, high-cost nature of conventional preparation methods, such as high-temperature solid-state reactions and prolonged hydrothermal synthesis, which limit production efficiency and industrial scalability. To address these challenges, this study investigates the synthesis and properties of sodium vanadium oxyfluorophosphate utilizing a green and scalable supercritical fluid processing route. The material was synthesized using a batch-type supercritical hydrothermal method at 400 °C with an exceptionally short residence time of 40 min, forming the nanoparticles in the range of 50–80 nm. Electrochemical analysis demonstrated that the synthesized material exhibited highly competitive kinetics. Cyclic voltammetry revealed two distinct V4+ to V5+ redox peaks between 3.5 and 3.6 V and 4 and 4.1 V as a two-step sodiation/desodiation process. The material displayed admirably low polarization hysteresis, with the initial discharge capacity reaching 108 mAh g–1 at a C/10 rate. The material demonstrated good rate capability, retaining 52 mAh g–1 at 10C and recovering 106 mAh g–1 at the C/10 rate, and the diffusion coefficient was quantified in the order of 10–10 to 10–11cm2 s–1. This work successfully establishes the supercritical fluid processing as a powerful, rapid, and high-efficiency platform for producing kinetically enhanced cathode materials, providing a critical reference for the future industrial development of high-power and long-lifespan Na-ion batteries.

title: Facilitating Charge Transport and Utilization in Mo-BiVO 4  via FeCo-Metal–Organic Framework Dual-Function Modification for Efficient Photoelectrochemical Water Splitting
content:
Abstract
The photoelectrochemical water splitting performance of BiVO4 photoanodes has historically been constrained by poor charge transport and sluggish water oxidation kinetics. Here, we design a heterojunction photoanode by coupling Mo-doped BiVO4 with a bimetallic FeCo-metal–organic framework (MOF) constructed using an extended π-conjugated linker (4,4′-biphenyldicarboxylic acid). The bimetallic FeCo-MOF based on the elongated backbone simultaneously serves as a hole-extraction layer that facilitates interfacial charge separation and an excellent oxygen evolution cocatalyst. It not only establishes an efficient charge transport channel but also plays a crucial role in improving the surface reaction kinetics. The optimized Mo-BiVO4/FeCo-MOF photoanode achieves a photocurrent density of 4.18 mA cm−2 at 1.23 V vs RHE and maintains stable operation for over 20 h, substantially outperforming pristine BiVO4. This work highlights the synergistic benefits of linker-engineered bimetallic MOF for high-performance solar water oxidation.
